A Houston native, Schaefer has long recruited the state of Texas throughout his coaching career. One of his best players at Mississippi State, center Teaira McCowan, the No. 3 pick in last year's WNBA draft, is from Texas.

He also has had success against Baylor. While an assistant specializing in defense at Texas A&M, he helped the Aggies defeat the Lady Bears in the 2011 Elite Eight and go on to win the NCAA title. At Mississippi State, his Bulldogs upset Baylor in the 2017 Elite Eight.

Schaefer started coaching at the high school level. He began his college coaching career as an assistant at Sam Houston State in 1987, then took over as head coach there in 1990. He became an assistant to Gary Blair at Arkansas in 1997, and then followed Blair to Texas A&M in 2003, before leaving for Mississippi State in 2012.

Schaefer and the Bulldogs went for a third consecutive Final Four last season, but lost in the Portland Regional final to Oregon. In 2017, Mississippi State had the biggest win in its program's history, when the Bulldogs ended UConn's 111-game win streak in the national semifinals in Dallas on Morgan William's buzzer-beating shot in overtime.

But Mississippi State then lost the 2017 NCAA final to the Gamecocks, who were the thorn in Schaefer's side during his time in Starkville, Mississippi. He went 3-12 against Dawn Staley's South Carolina program, losing in the SEC tournament championship game four of the past five years to the Gamecocks.

Schaefer did have several program-breakthrough victories, including Mississippi State's first win over Tennessee in 2016 after the Bulldogs had gone 0-36 all time against the Lady Vols, and last year's SEC tournament title, the first for Mississippi State. The Bulldogs beat Arkansas in that final.

Over the past five seasons, Mississippi State is third in overall victory total with 159, following UConn's 174 and Baylor's 167. Mississippi State was 6-6 in the NCAA tournament before Schaefer took over. He went 16-5 in five NCAA tournament appearances.

Schaefer will be the first male head coach to lead the Longhorns program since Page in the 1970s. Texas now has only two women head coaches (swimming and diving and soccer) across its athletic program.

# Vic Schaefer leaves Mississippi State to be Texas women's coach

!Image 3play

UConn's 111-game win streak comes to an end at the hands of MSU (1:55)

*   Mechelle Voepel 

Multiple Authors

Apr 5, 2020, 04:17 PM ET

![Image 4](https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/content-reactions/share-ios-on_light.png&h=80&w=80)Share

*   [Copy Link![Image 5: Copy Link](https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/content-reactions/check.png&h=80&w=80)](https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/story/_/id/28997584/texas-hires-mississippi-state-vic-schaefer-new-head-coach#)
*   [Email](mailto:?subject=Vic%20Schaefer%20leaves%20Mississippi%20State%20to%20be%20Texas%20women%27s%20coach&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.espn.com%2Fwomens%2Dcollege%2Dbasketball%2Fstory%2F_%2Fid%2F28997584)
*   [Print](https://www.espn.com/espn/print?id=28997584)

Vic Schaefer is the new women's basketball coach at Texas, after spending the past eight seasons building a powerhouse at Mississippi State.

"I certainly feel really fortunate and just truly humbled to be entrusted with the opportunity to build on the years of success and help lead the Longhorns back where they belong -- among the nation's elite," Schaefer said in a statement.

Texas athletic director Chris Del Conte first broke the news in a [tweet](https://twitter.com/_delconte/status/1246881499607154691?s=20) on Sunday of Schaefer and his family giving the "Hook 'em Horns" sign with the words, "Guess who's coming to the Forty" referencing Texas' nickname as the Forty Acres.

Schaefer, a Texas native, graduated from Texas A&M and spent nine years as associate head coach there under coach Gary Blair. He was a member of the Aggies' staff when they won the national championship in 2011.

1 Related

He took over as head coach of Mississippi State in 2012 and led the Bulldogs to the national championship game in 2017 and 2018, losing both times.

Schaefer replaces Karen Aston, who was 184-83 at Texas. Del Conte announced Friday that her contract, which expires in August, would not be renewed.

"In looking for a new head women's basketball coach, there was one name that continuously came up as the perfect fit for The University of Texas, and that was Vic Schaefer," Del Conte said in a statement Sunday. "He's a coach who knows the state of Texas and the national women's college basketball landscape extremely well."

Schaefer, who turned 59 in March, has gone 221-62 in his eight seasons with the Bulldogs, which includes the regular season and SEC tournament this year. He becomes the fifth women's basketball coach in Texas history, following Rod Page, Jody Conradt, Gail Goestenkors and Aston.

Texas won the 1986 NCAA title with a perfect season under Conradt, and she also led the program to two other NCAA Women's Final Fours, most recently in 2003. But the Longhorns have been eclipsed in the Big 12 by three-time NCAA champ Baylor, which has gone 22-1 against Texas in the past decade.

Aston was 1-18 against the Lady Bears, which was a big contributing factor to why she was let go despite three Sweet 16 appearances and one Elite Eight appearance in her eight seasons as head coach.

Texas went 19-11 overall this past season, and was third in the Big 12 at 11-7. Mississippi State went 27-6 overall and was second in the SEC at 13-3.

## Winning When it Counts

Vic Schaefer went 16-5 with Mississippi State in the NCAA Tournament, good for the third-best winning percentage among coaches.

A Houston native, Schaefer has long recruited the state of Texas throughout his coaching career. One of his best players at Mississippi State, center Teaira McCowan, the No. 3 pick in last year's WNBA draft, is from Texas.

He also has had success against Baylor. While an assistant specializing in defense at Texas A&M, he helped the Aggies defeat the Lady Bears in the 2011 Elite Eight and go on to win the NCAA title. At Mississippi State, his Bulldogs upset Baylor in the 2017 Elite Eight.

Schaefer started coaching at the high school level. He began his college coaching career as an assistant at Sam Houston State in 1987, then took over as head coach there in 1990. He became an assistant to Gary Blair at Arkansas in 1997, and then followed Blair to Texas A&M in 2003, before leaving for Mississippi State in 2012.

Schaefer and the Bulldogs went for a third consecutive Final Four last season, but lost in the Portland Regional final to Oregon. In 2017, Mississippi State had the biggest win in its program's history, when the Bulldogs ended UConn's 111-game win streak in the national semifinals in Dallas on Morgan William's buzzer-beating shot in overtime.

But Mississippi State then lost the 2017 NCAA final to the Gamecocks, who were the thorn in Schaefer's side during his time in Starkville, Mississippi. He went 3-12 against Dawn Staley's South Carolina program, losing in the SEC tournament championship game four of the past five years to the Gamecocks.

Schaefer did have several program-breakthrough victories, including Mississippi State's first win over Tennessee in 2016 after the Bulldogs had gone 0-36 all time against the Lady Vols, and last year's SEC tournament title, the first for Mississippi State. The Bulldogs beat Arkansas in that final.

Over the past five seasons, Mississippi State is third in overall victory total with 159, following UConn's 174 and Baylor's 167. Mississippi State was 6-6 in the NCAA tournament before Schaefer took over. He went 16-5 in five NCAA tournament appearances.

Schaefer will be the first male head coach to lead the Longhorns program since Page in the 1970s. Texas now has only two women head coaches (swimming and diving and soccer) across its athletic program.

# Texas women’s basketball head coach Vic Schaefer ready to move on after first loss of the season

[Sophia Sandoval](https://thedailytexan.com/staff_name/sophia-sandoval/), Sports desk editor

January 13, 2026

[![Image 14: Fans high-five the Longhorns as they run out onto the court for the second half of a game against Auburn on Thursday, Jan. 8. The Longhorns went on to win the game with a final score of 97-36.](https://thedailytexan.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/1-13-26_WBBMediaAvail_YsaMendoza_11-1200x800.jpg)](https://thedailytexan.com/2026/01/13/texas-womens-basketball-head-coach-vic-schaefer-ready-to-move-on-after-first-loss-of-the-season/#photo)

[Ysa Mendoza](https://thedailytexan.com/staff_name/ysa-mendoza/)

Fans high-five the Longhorns as they run out onto the court for the second half of a game against Auburn on Thursday, Jan. 8. The Longhorns went on to win the game with a final score of 97-36.

After Texas women’s basketball took its first loss of the season against LSU, head coach Vic Schaefer insisted the game plan was there.

The execution, however, was certainly not.

Schaefer pointed to a breakdown not in preparation, but in discipline. Texas looked uncharacteristically out of sync and sloppy, plagued by turnovers and the inability to match LSU’s physicality on the floor. These issues are rarely seen in a Schaefer team.

Advertisement

  

Texas entered the game averaging a Division I-low 10.2 turnovers per contest, according to ESPN, but committed a season-high 17 against the Tigers. LSU’s aggressive pressure disrupted the Longhorns’ rhythm early, stalling an offense that struggled to find consistency.

Regardless of what went wrong Sunday and who is at fault, Texas has little time to dwell on it. The Longhorns now turn their attention to Thursday’s matchup against No. 2 South Carolina, a team they defeated in November in Las Vegas.

That win, as impressive as it was, carries little weight now. November basketball is worlds different from January basketball, especially as Texas awaits another hostile environment in Columbia.

The quick turnaround from LSU to South Carolina is something Schaefer openly criticized, questioning the Southeastern Conference’s decision to schedule two of the league’s top teams back-to-back on the road. It’s a critique he has voiced before, as he feels Texas constantly gets the short end of the stick when it comes to scheduling.

Regardless of criticism, committing to Texas means committing to the competitiveness of the league. The SEC remains a gauntlet of elite teams, filled with future WNBA players and Hall of Fame coaches, and Texas still faces a demanding schedule as the season approaches its midway point. An undefeated conference run was never realistic, so the concern is not necessarily the loss, but the manner in which it happened.

While the issues of the team lacking discipline and playing selfishly at times need to be addressed before Thursday, Schaefer said that the first step — accountability — starts with him.

“I thought we had a great plan, we just did not execute, and so again, I obviously fell short in that area of getting my team ready to go play there,” Schaefer said. “I wear that, I’m accountable. That’s just who I am. I don’t run from that. It’s how I was raised. … And it’s not just a kid problem. It’s an adult problem, too. I see it every day, but at the end of the day, I try to be accountable. And if I’m wrong, I’m wrong.”

The preparation, he insisted, is there. The practices are there. What remains is translating that work when it matters most.

Thursday’s matchup against South Carolina will test Texas’ ability to move past a disappointing loss and respond with the discipline and toughness Schaefer expects and demands from his team.

“I’m ready to move on,” Schaefer said. “When the lights come on, I’m always ready to go. But I’m ready to go when that game’s over, I’m moving on to the next one. … It’s tough, you know, having to do this. But you know, my kids will be ready. They’ll be focused, they’ll embrace the challenge that we have and we’ll go play.”

# Texas women’s basketball head coach Vic Schaefer ready to move on after first loss of the season

[Sophia Sandoval](https://thedailytexan.com/staff_name/sophia-sandoval/), Sports desk editor

January 13, 2026

[![Image 14: Fans high-five the Longhorns as they run out onto the court for the second half of a game against Auburn on Thursday, Jan. 8. The Longhorns went on to win the game with a final score of 97-36.](https://thedailytexan.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/1-13-26_WBBMediaAvail_YsaMendoza_11-1200x800.jpg)](https://thedailytexan.com/2026/01/13/texas-womens-basketball-head-coach-vic-schaefer-ready-to-move-on-after-first-loss-of-the-season/#photo)

[Ysa Mendoza](https://thedailytexan.com/staff_name/ysa-mendoza/)

Fans high-five the Longhorns as they run out onto the court for the second half of a game against Auburn on Thursday, Jan. 8. The Longhorns went on to win the game with a final score of 97-36.

After Texas women’s basketball took its first loss of the season against LSU, head coach Vic Schaefer insisted the game plan was there.

The execution, however, was certainly not.

Schaefer pointed to a breakdown not in preparation, but in discipline. Texas looked uncharacteristically out of sync and sloppy, plagued by turnovers and the inability to match LSU’s physicality on the floor. These issues are rarely seen in a Schaefer team.

Advertisement

  

Texas entered the game averaging a Division I-low 10.2 turnovers per contest, according to ESPN, but committed a season-high 17 against the Tigers. LSU’s aggressive pressure disrupted the Longhorns’ rhythm early, stalling an offense that struggled to find consistency.

Regardless of what went wrong Sunday and who is at fault, Texas has little time to dwell on it. The Longhorns now turn their attention to Thursday’s matchup against No. 2 South Carolina, a team they defeated in November in Las Vegas.

That win, as impressive as it was, carries little weight now. November basketball is worlds different from January basketball, especially as Texas awaits another hostile environment in Columbia.

The quick turnaround from LSU to South Carolina is something Schaefer openly criticized, questioning the Southeastern Conference’s decision to schedule two of the league’s top teams back-to-back on the road. It’s a critique he has voiced before, as he feels Texas constantly gets the short end of the stick when it comes to scheduling.

Regardless of criticism, committing to Texas means committing to the competitiveness of the league. The SEC remains a gauntlet of elite teams, filled with future WNBA players and Hall of Fame coaches, and Texas still faces a demanding schedule as the season approaches its midway point. An undefeated conference run was never realistic, so the concern is not necessarily the loss, but the manner in which it happened.

While the issues of the team lacking discipline and playing selfishly at times need to be addressed before Thursday, Schaefer said that the first step — accountability — starts with him.

“I thought we had a great plan, we just did not execute, and so again, I obviously fell short in that area of getting my team ready to go play there,” Schaefer said. “I wear that, I’m accountable. That’s just who I am. I don’t run from that. It’s how I was raised. … And it’s not just a kid problem. It’s an adult problem, too. I see it every day, but at the end of the day, I try to be accountable. And if I’m wrong, I’m wrong.”

The preparation, he insisted, is there. The practices are there. What remains is translating that work when it matters most.

Thursday’s matchup against South Carolina will test Texas’ ability to move past a disappointing loss and respond with the discipline and toughness Schaefer expects and demands from his team.

“I’m ready to move on,” Schaefer said. “When the lights come on, I’m always ready to go. But I’m ready to go when that game’s over, I’m moving on to the next one. … It’s tough, you know, having to do this. But you know, my kids will be ready. They’ll be focused, they’ll embrace the challenge that we have and we’ll go play.”

The **Texas Longhorns women's basketball team** represents the [University of Texas at Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") in [NCAA Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I")[intercollegiate women's basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_basketball "College basketball") competition. The Longhorns compete in the [SEC Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEC_Conference "SEC Conference").

Under head coach [Jody Conradt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jody_Conradt "Jody Conradt"), the second [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association") Division I basketball coach to win 900 career games (after [Tennessee's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball "Tennessee Lady Volunteers basketball")[Pat Summitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Summitt "Pat Summitt")), the Longhorns won the 1986 national championship. Conradt retired after the 2006–07 season, and was replaced by [Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Blue_Devils "Duke Blue Devils") head coach [Gail Goestenkors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gail_Goestenkors "Gail Goestenkors"). She resigned after five seasons and was replaced by [Karen Aston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Aston "Karen Aston"), whose contract was not renewed following the 2019–20 season. In April 2020, [Vic Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Schaefer "Vic Schaefer") was named the program's fifth head coach.

From 1977 to 2022, Texas women's basketball played its home games in the [Frank Erwin Special Events Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Erwin_Center "Frank Erwin Center"), where the team compiled a 576–118 (.830) record. The final game played in the Erwin Center was an NCAA second-round victory over Utah, 78–56, on March 20, 2022. Since the start of the 2022–23 season, the team has played in the $388 million [Moody Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Center "Moody Center").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[The University of Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") held its first basketball competition in 1900, six years before Magnus Mainland started the men's team at Texas. The games in the first few years were intramural. By 1906, the school was playing other institutions, although only home games, not off-campus.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2) Full varsity intercollegiate competition in women's [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") began in 1974. Through the 2021–22 season, the [Longhorns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns "Texas Longhorns") rank sixth in total victories and eighth in all-time win percentage among all [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA "NCAA")[Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_I_(NCAA) "Division I (NCAA)")[women's college basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_basketball "Women's basketball") programs, with an all-time win–loss record of 1161–424 (.732).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-2021-22_Postseason_Media_Guide-3)

The Longhorns have won 22 total conference championships (12 regular-season conference titles and 10 conference tournament titles) in women's basketball and have made 38 total appearances in the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Women's_Division_I_Basketball_Championship "NCAA Women's Division I Basketball Championship") (57–35 overall record),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-4) reaching the [NCAA Final Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Women's_Division_I_Basketball_Championship "NCAA Women's Division I Basketball Championship") five times (1986, 1987, 2003, 2025, 2026) and the [NCAA regional finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elite_Eight "Elite Eight") ([Elite Eight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elite_Eight "Elite Eight")) 14 times.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-5) Texas won the [1986 NCAA Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "1986 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") to finish the 1985–86 season with a 34–0 record. Through the 2021–22 season, Texas ranks 10th in all-time NCAA Tournament victories (48), trailing [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut_Huskies_women's_basketball "Connecticut Huskies women's basketball") (130), [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball "Tennessee Lady Volunteers basketball") (128), [Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Cardinal_women's_basketball "Stanford Cardinal women's basketball") (99), [Notre Dame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball "Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball") (69), [Louisiana Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Tech_Lady_Techsters_basketball "Louisiana Tech Lady Techsters basketball") (65), [Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Blue_Devils "Duke Blue Devils") (61), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Lady_Bulldogs_basketball "Georgia Lady Bulldogs basketball") (58), [Baylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_Lady_Bears_basketball "Baylor Lady Bears basketball") (54) and [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_Tar_Heels_women's_basketball "North Carolina Tar Heels women's basketball") (49).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Texas_Quick_Facts-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-7)

### Early years (1900–1966)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years (1900–1966)")]

The very first women's basketball games occurred in 1892, at [Smith College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith_College "Smith College"), under the direction of [Senda Berenson Abbott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senda_Berenson_Abbott "Senda Berenson Abbott"). Shortly thereafter, [Clara Baer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Gregory_Baer "Clara Gregory Baer") brought the game to Louisiana. The details of how the game came to Texas is not known for certain, but in 1900, Eleanore Norvell organized the first basketball game at the University of Texas. Norvell was originally from Oklahoma, and came to Texas to direct the physical education department. She has been at Texas for less than a year when she introduced basketball to students at the school. The first recorded game occurred on Saturday January 13, 1900. The teams played four ten-minute quarters—the final score of that first game was 3–2.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2)

Although the men's game and women's game both had their roots in the Naismith [rules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rules_of_basketball "Rules of basketball"), the first set of rules left a lot to be specified, and the rules for the women's game developed differently than for the men. Both Senda Berensen and Clara Baer used Naismith's rules as an inspiration, but developed their own set of rules, including marked areas on the court limiting the movement of players to their respective sections. Some of these rules were motivated by the prevailing assumptions of "female frailty and dependence".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Shackleford_and_Grundy15-8)

Texas would play limited intercollegiate basketball between 1903 and 1921. Eunice Aden was captain of the basketball team in 1903, took over coaching duties in 1905 and became director of physical education in 1911. Opportunities in basketball grew, but only in a limited way. Intercollegiate play existed, but the school did not allow off-campus games. When Aden retired in 1921, she was replaced by Anna Hiss, who would run the physical education department until 1957. While she was called a visionary for her role in directing physical education and intramurals, she was "dead-set against intercollegiate athletics for women". The limited intercollegiate play under Aden came to an end, with basketball now limited to intramurals and interclass play.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2)

The ascension of Hiss to the head of the department roughly coincided with the influence of [Lou Henry Hoover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Henry_Hoover "Lou Henry Hoover"), First Lady of the United States. In 1923, Hoover was head of the [Girl Scouts of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girl_Scouts_of_the_United_States "Girl Scouts of the United States"). Although Hoover was an advocate of sports, she felt that highly competitive sports were detrimental.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Lannin-9) Hoover helped to found the Women's Division of the National Amateur Athletic Foundation (WDNAAF). This foundation passed a resolution in 1925 banning extramural competition.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Lannin-9) The following year, Hiss formed an organization which voted "condemn intercollegiate competition for women, and to endorse the intramural/interclass model".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2)

Hiss supported many activities, including tennis, golf, archery, swimming and interpretive dance, but was opposed to team sports. In general, "artistry was favored over athleticism".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2) She led an unsuccessful protest against American woman participation in the Olympics of 1928, 1932, and 1936. She was the driving force behind the construction of a Women's Gymnasium (named in her honor after her death). While it was a substantial resource for women's athletics, it was designed to fit her beliefs—the courts were too small for a proper basketball game, and had no room for spectators and the swimming pool was deliberately shorter than Olympic length.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2)

While basketball was not officially supported as a school-sponsored sport in the 1920s and 30s, it was still played by many groups. The interclass games were de-emphasized, but fraternities and sororities played the game, as well as organizations such as the YWCA, industrial leagues and AAU teams.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2)

### Intermediate years (1967–1974) Club Level

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Intermediate years (1967–1974) Club Level")]

After Hiss's departure, basketball at Texas began to grow, although it would be almost a decade until it became a full varsity sport. The University of Texas Sports Association (UTSA) a predecessor to the athletic department, organized the sports available for women. Basketball was not one of the club sports offered until a student, Mary Neikirk, organized a petition which was presented to the administration. The school agreed to add basketball as a club sport under the auspices of the UTSA.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1967-10)

The first year's budget was $100. A team was formed, and the team played under the girl's rules of the era—six players on a team, two of whom stayed at the defensive end, two of whom stayed in the offensive end and two, called "rovers" who could play both ends. These rules were used until 1971, at which time they switched to "boy's rules".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1967-10)

In 1973, the team practiced and played in the annex of [Gregory Gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_Gymnasium "Gregory Gymnasium"). [Rodney Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodney_Page "Rodney Page"), who had some experience as a women's basketball assistant coach, was a referee at one of the games. When the current coach of the team quit, Page was hired. The Texas team, in Pages' first year, compiled a record of 7–11.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1967-10)

The 1974 season was a season of transition, with a mixture of firsts and lasts. This year's team was the first to play their games in Gregory Gymnasium itself, rather than the annex. This was the first year the team had trainers, and it was the first year that the Longhorn Band and cheerleaders perform for the team. It was their last year under the auspices of the UTSA. It was the last year before the sport attained the status of a full varsity sport.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1967-10)

[Title IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_IX "Title IX") was passed in 1972, with a provision prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sex. At the time it was passed, it was unknown what impact it would have on sports, including whether it even applied to intercollegiate sports.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Festle-11) Two years, later, in 1974, the issue wasn't yet settled, with the Tower Amendment specifically excluding revenue-producing sports,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Legislative_History-12) but shortly thereafter, the Tower Amendment was eliminated.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-compliance-13) It was becoming clear that universities would have to respond sooner or later, but Texas responded in 1974. Shortly after the conclusion of the 1974 basketball season, Stephen Spurr, the university president, announced that a women's athletic department would be started, complete with offices, staff and a budget of $50,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1967-10)

### Rod Page years (1974–1976)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Rod Page years (1974–1976)")]

Some schools waited for the Department of Health, Education and Welfare to provide specific regulations covering Title IX. These regulations would not be published until 1975. In 1974, Texas began offering varsity sports opportunities to female students in seven sports.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1975-14) In some ways, the University of Texas program became the envy of women at other schools, but the initial progress was relative. Two-thirds of the male athletes at Texas were on scholarship, while only one in fifteen female students were on scholarship. There were 21 male coach positions, almost all full-time, but seven women's coaches who were all part-time.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Festle-11)

In the team's debut year, 1974–75, the team improved on their prior year's record, put together their first winning season by and they won the Texas State Invitational. The team started out strong, winning their first five games, including an overtime win against Houston 63–62, before running into Baylor, who won easily 116–62. Some of the games were played as preliminaries to the men's games, but others were stand-alone games.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1975-14) They would also lose their next game to [Southwest Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_State_Bobcats "Texas State Bobcats"), on a night when fundraiser was held, with an exhibition match between UT All-Stars and the [All American Red Heads Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_American_Red_Heads_Team "All American Red Heads Team"), a barnstorming team of female basketball players. The team earned an invitation to the Texas [AIAW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIAW "AIAW") post season tournament, as a second seed behind Southwest Texas. The tournament schedule required five games in three days. The Texas team did well, except against Southwest Texas, ending up with 17 victories against 10 losses, five of which were to Southwest Texas.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1975-14) Despite a winning record, they failed to make the [AIAW tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_AIAW_National_Basketball_Championship "1974 AIAW National Basketball Championship").

The following season, Texas team would achieve even more. The basketball team added [Retha Swindell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retha_Swindell "Retha Swindell"), a 6' 2" rebounder with defensive skills. The school also hired [Donna Lopiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donna_Lopiano "Donna Lopiano"), who started what would become a 17-year stint as women's athletic director. She "vowed to have every Longhorn women's team in the top 10 and at least one national title within five years".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1976-15) While the school was expressing a commitment to women's varsity sports, not everyone was supportive. The football coach, [Darrell Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darrell_Royal "Darrell Royal"), had told President Ford that "Title IX might be the death of big-time college football.".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1976-15) Despite that concern, she managed to convince him to support her during her interview. The team's first game was against Southwest Texas, the team that had defeated Texas five times in the previous season. This time, Texas would prevail 57–47 in a game held at their arena. The team lost three in a row as a result of sickness and injury, then responded with a twelve-game winning streak. The team would go on to a 21–7 season record and finish 1st in the Texas AIAW South Central Zone.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1976-15)

Under Rod Page, the team had improved materially, so it was a surprise that when the Longhorns completed their regular season and prepared for the post-season tournament, athletic director Lopiano announced he would not be continuing as coach of the team. The news came as a shock to Page and the team. The reason given was that the position was a head coach of basketball and volleyball—Page did not have volleyball experience. However, Lopiano had her eye on Jody Conradt, who she felt could lead the team to become a national contender.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1976-15)
