The **Texas Longhorns women's basketball team** represents the [University of Texas at Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") in [NCAA Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I")[intercollegiate women's basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_basketball "College basketball") competition. The Longhorns compete in the [SEC Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEC_Conference "SEC Conference").

Under head coach [Jody Conradt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jody_Conradt "Jody Conradt"), the second [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association") Division I basketball coach to win 900 career games (after [Tennessee's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball "Tennessee Lady Volunteers basketball")[Pat Summitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Summitt "Pat Summitt")), the Longhorns won the 1986 national championship. Conradt retired after the 2006–07 season, and was replaced by [Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Blue_Devils "Duke Blue Devils") head coach [Gail Goestenkors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gail_Goestenkors "Gail Goestenkors"). She resigned after five seasons and was replaced by [Karen Aston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Aston "Karen Aston"), whose contract was not renewed following the 2019–20 season. In April 2020, [Vic Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Schaefer "Vic Schaefer") was named the program's fifth head coach.

From 1977 to 2022, Texas women's basketball played its home games in the [Frank Erwin Special Events Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Erwin_Center "Frank Erwin Center"), where the team compiled a 576–118 (.830) record. The final game played in the Erwin Center was an NCAA second-round victory over Utah, 78–56, on March 20, 2022. Since the start of the 2022–23 season, the team has played in the $388 million [Moody Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Center "Moody Center").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[The University of Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") held its first basketball competition in 1900, six years before Magnus Mainland started the men's team at Texas. The games in the first few years were intramural. By 1906, the school was playing other institutions, although only home games, not off-campus.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2) Full varsity intercollegiate competition in women's [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") began in 1974. Through the 2021–22 season, the [Longhorns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns "Texas Longhorns") rank sixth in total victories and eighth in all-time win percentage among all [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA "NCAA")[Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_I_(NCAA) "Division I (NCAA)")[women's college basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_basketball "Women's basketball") programs, with an all-time win–loss record of 1161–424 (.732).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-2021-22_Postseason_Media_Guide-3)

The Longhorns have won 22 total conference championships (12 regular-season conference titles and 10 conference tournament titles) in women's basketball and have made 38 total appearances in the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Women's_Division_I_Basketball_Championship "NCAA Women's Division I Basketball Championship") (57–35 overall record),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-4) reaching the [NCAA Final Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Women's_Division_I_Basketball_Championship "NCAA Women's Division I Basketball Championship") five times (1986, 1987, 2003, 2025, 2026) and the [NCAA regional finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elite_Eight "Elite Eight") ([Elite Eight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elite_Eight "Elite Eight")) 14 times.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-5) Texas won the [1986 NCAA Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "1986 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") to finish the 1985–86 season with a 34–0 record. Through the 2021–22 season, Texas ranks 10th in all-time NCAA Tournament victories (48), trailing [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut_Huskies_women's_basketball "Connecticut Huskies women's basketball") (130), [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball "Tennessee Lady Volunteers basketball") (128), [Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Cardinal_women's_basketball "Stanford Cardinal women's basketball") (99), [Notre Dame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball "Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball") (69), [Louisiana Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Tech_Lady_Techsters_basketball "Louisiana Tech Lady Techsters basketball") (65), [Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Blue_Devils "Duke Blue Devils") (61), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Lady_Bulldogs_basketball "Georgia Lady Bulldogs basketball") (58), [Baylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_Lady_Bears_basketball "Baylor Lady Bears basketball") (54) and [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_Tar_Heels_women's_basketball "North Carolina Tar Heels women's basketball") (49).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Texas_Quick_Facts-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-7)

### Early years (1900–1966)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years (1900–1966)")]

The very first women's basketball games occurred in 1892, at [Smith College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith_College "Smith College"), under the direction of [Senda Berenson Abbott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senda_Berenson_Abbott "Senda Berenson Abbott"). Shortly thereafter, [Clara Baer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Gregory_Baer "Clara Gregory Baer") brought the game to Louisiana. The details of how the game came to Texas is not known for certain, but in 1900, Eleanore Norvell organized the first basketball game at the University of Texas. Norvell was originally from Oklahoma, and came to Texas to direct the physical education department. She has been at Texas for less than a year when she introduced basketball to students at the school. The first recorded game occurred on Saturday January 13, 1900. The teams played four ten-minute quarters—the final score of that first game was 3–2.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2)

Although the men's game and women's game both had their roots in the Naismith [rules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rules_of_basketball "Rules of basketball"), the first set of rules left a lot to be specified, and the rules for the women's game developed differently than for the men. Both Senda Berensen and Clara Baer used Naismith's rules as an inspiration, but developed their own set of rules, including marked areas on the court limiting the movement of players to their respective sections. Some of these rules were motivated by the prevailing assumptions of "female frailty and dependence".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Shackleford_and_Grundy15-8)

Texas would play limited intercollegiate basketball between 1903 and 1921. Eunice Aden was captain of the basketball team in 1903, took over coaching duties in 1905 and became director of physical education in 1911. Opportunities in basketball grew, but only in a limited way. Intercollegiate play existed, but the school did not allow off-campus games. When Aden retired in 1921, she was replaced by Anna Hiss, who would run the physical education department until 1957. While she was called a visionary for her role in directing physical education and intramurals, she was "dead-set against intercollegiate athletics for women". The limited intercollegiate play under Aden came to an end, with basketball now limited to intramurals and interclass play.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2)

The ascension of Hiss to the head of the department roughly coincided with the influence of [Lou Henry Hoover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Henry_Hoover "Lou Henry Hoover"), First Lady of the United States. In 1923, Hoover was head of the [Girl Scouts of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girl_Scouts_of_the_United_States "Girl Scouts of the United States"). Although Hoover was an advocate of sports, she felt that highly competitive sports were detrimental.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Lannin-9) Hoover helped to found the Women's Division of the National Amateur Athletic Foundation (WDNAAF). This foundation passed a resolution in 1925 banning extramural competition.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Lannin-9) The following year, Hiss formed an organization which voted "condemn intercollegiate competition for women, and to endorse the intramural/interclass model".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2)

Hiss supported many activities, including tennis, golf, archery, swimming and interpretive dance, but was opposed to team sports. In general, "artistry was favored over athleticism".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2) She led an unsuccessful protest against American woman participation in the Olympics of 1928, 1932, and 1936. She was the driving force behind the construction of a Women's Gymnasium (named in her honor after her death). While it was a substantial resource for women's athletics, it was designed to fit her beliefs—the courts were too small for a proper basketball game, and had no room for spectators and the swimming pool was deliberately shorter than Olympic length.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2)

While basketball was not officially supported as a school-sponsored sport in the 1920s and 30s, it was still played by many groups. The interclass games were de-emphasized, but fraternities and sororities played the game, as well as organizations such as the YWCA, industrial leagues and AAU teams.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1900-2)

### Intermediate years (1967–1974) Club Level

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Intermediate years (1967–1974) Club Level")]

After Hiss's departure, basketball at Texas began to grow, although it would be almost a decade until it became a full varsity sport. The University of Texas Sports Association (UTSA) a predecessor to the athletic department, organized the sports available for women. Basketball was not one of the club sports offered until a student, Mary Neikirk, organized a petition which was presented to the administration. The school agreed to add basketball as a club sport under the auspices of the UTSA.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1967-10)

The first year's budget was $100. A team was formed, and the team played under the girl's rules of the era—six players on a team, two of whom stayed at the defensive end, two of whom stayed in the offensive end and two, called "rovers" who could play both ends. These rules were used until 1971, at which time they switched to "boy's rules".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1967-10)

In 1973, the team practiced and played in the annex of [Gregory Gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_Gymnasium "Gregory Gymnasium"). [Rodney Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodney_Page "Rodney Page"), who had some experience as a women's basketball assistant coach, was a referee at one of the games. When the current coach of the team quit, Page was hired. The Texas team, in Pages' first year, compiled a record of 7–11.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1967-10)

The 1974 season was a season of transition, with a mixture of firsts and lasts. This year's team was the first to play their games in Gregory Gymnasium itself, rather than the annex. This was the first year the team had trainers, and it was the first year that the Longhorn Band and cheerleaders perform for the team. It was their last year under the auspices of the UTSA. It was the last year before the sport attained the status of a full varsity sport.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1967-10)

[Title IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_IX "Title IX") was passed in 1972, with a provision prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sex. At the time it was passed, it was unknown what impact it would have on sports, including whether it even applied to intercollegiate sports.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Festle-11) Two years, later, in 1974, the issue wasn't yet settled, with the Tower Amendment specifically excluding revenue-producing sports,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Legislative_History-12) but shortly thereafter, the Tower Amendment was eliminated.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-compliance-13) It was becoming clear that universities would have to respond sooner or later, but Texas responded in 1974. Shortly after the conclusion of the 1974 basketball season, Stephen Spurr, the university president, announced that a women's athletic department would be started, complete with offices, staff and a budget of $50,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1967-10)

### Rod Page years (1974–1976)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Rod Page years (1974–1976)")]

Some schools waited for the Department of Health, Education and Welfare to provide specific regulations covering Title IX. These regulations would not be published until 1975. In 1974, Texas began offering varsity sports opportunities to female students in seven sports.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1975-14) In some ways, the University of Texas program became the envy of women at other schools, but the initial progress was relative. Two-thirds of the male athletes at Texas were on scholarship, while only one in fifteen female students were on scholarship. There were 21 male coach positions, almost all full-time, but seven women's coaches who were all part-time.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Festle-11)

In the team's debut year, 1974–75, the team improved on their prior year's record, put together their first winning season by and they won the Texas State Invitational. The team started out strong, winning their first five games, including an overtime win against Houston 63–62, before running into Baylor, who won easily 116–62. Some of the games were played as preliminaries to the men's games, but others were stand-alone games.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1975-14) They would also lose their next game to [Southwest Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_State_Bobcats "Texas State Bobcats"), on a night when fundraiser was held, with an exhibition match between UT All-Stars and the [All American Red Heads Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_American_Red_Heads_Team "All American Red Heads Team"), a barnstorming team of female basketball players. The team earned an invitation to the Texas [AIAW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIAW "AIAW") post season tournament, as a second seed behind Southwest Texas. The tournament schedule required five games in three days. The Texas team did well, except against Southwest Texas, ending up with 17 victories against 10 losses, five of which were to Southwest Texas.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1975-14) Despite a winning record, they failed to make the [AIAW tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_AIAW_National_Basketball_Championship "1974 AIAW National Basketball Championship").

The following season, Texas team would achieve even more. The basketball team added [Retha Swindell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retha_Swindell "Retha Swindell"), a 6' 2" rebounder with defensive skills. The school also hired [Donna Lopiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donna_Lopiano "Donna Lopiano"), who started what would become a 17-year stint as women's athletic director. She "vowed to have every Longhorn women's team in the top 10 and at least one national title within five years".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1976-15) While the school was expressing a commitment to women's varsity sports, not everyone was supportive. The football coach, [Darrell Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darrell_Royal "Darrell Royal"), had told President Ford that "Title IX might be the death of big-time college football.".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1976-15) Despite that concern, she managed to convince him to support her during her interview. The team's first game was against Southwest Texas, the team that had defeated Texas five times in the previous season. This time, Texas would prevail 57–47 in a game held at their arena. The team lost three in a row as a result of sickness and injury, then responded with a twelve-game winning streak. The team would go on to a 21–7 season record and finish 1st in the Texas AIAW South Central Zone.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1976-15)

Under Rod Page, the team had improved materially, so it was a surprise that when the Longhorns completed their regular season and prepared for the post-season tournament, athletic director Lopiano announced he would not be continuing as coach of the team. The news came as a shock to Page and the team. The reason given was that the position was a head coach of basketball and volleyball—Page did not have volleyball experience. However, Lopiano had her eye on Jody Conradt, who she felt could lead the team to become a national contender.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1976-15)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Jody_conradt.jpg/250px-Jody_conradt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jody_conradt.jpg)

[Jody Conradt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jody_Conradt "Jody Conradt"), head coach from 1976 to 2007

### Jody Conradt era (1976–2007)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Jody Conradt era (1976–2007)")]

#### Independent

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Independent")]

Lopiano's choice was [Jody Conradt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jody_Conradt "Jody Conradt"), who was garnering national attention as the head coach at the [University of Texas at Arlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Arlington "University of Texas at Arlington"). She turned a losing program around, and the 1975–76 team would compile a 23–11 record, despite materially strengthening their schedule of opponents at the same time.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-porter-16) Two days after announcing that Page would not be returning, Lopiano announced that Conradt would be the coach starting with the next season. Conradt wasn't surprised that the team felt loyalty to Page, but she asked them to "have an open mind".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1977-17)

The first season under Conradt 1976-77 had a schedule of 46 games. The schedule included games in the Northeast, the first out-of-state trip for the team, and the first airplane ride for many of the players. To save money, the team stayed at the home of Lopiano's parents in [Stamford, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamford,_Connecticut "Stamford, Connecticut"). Texas lost badly to [Queens College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens_College "Queens College"), then ranked No. 15 in the nation, but went on to the Penn State Invitational where they beat [Penn State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_State "Penn State") and [Southern Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Connecticut "Southern Connecticut"), at that time a national power.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1977-17)[Mel Greenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_Greenberg "Mel Greenberg"), the organizer of the first top 25 women's poll, was in attendance. By the time the team returned to Austin, it learned of its first national ranking at No. 14. The team would complete its first season under Conradt with a record of 36–10 and make its first ever trip to the AIAW Regional Tournament.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1977-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-wbbrecord-18)

In 1977–78, Texas went 29–10, finished first in the Texas AIAW S.C. Zone and went to the AIAW Regional Tournament again. They then made their first and only trip to the [National Women's Invitational Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Women's_Invitational_Tournament "National Women's Invitational Tournament") where they made it to the championship game and lost to [Old Dominion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dominion_Monarchs_women's_basketball "Old Dominion Monarchs women's basketball") to finish ranked #15 - their first end of season ranking in program history.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-19)

Conradt coached both basketball and volleyball her first two seasons, but would give up volleyball duties after the 1977–78 season.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Pennington_1978-20) The team would go on to become a dominant women's basketball team on the 1980s, ranked in the AP Top 10 for all but one year between 1979 and 1990.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-porter-16)

1978-79 was the program's best season up to that point. They won a then-school record 37 games and had their best ever winning percentage of 0.902. They went to the AIAW regional for the third time in a row, but despite finishing the season ranked at a best ever #4 in the AP Poll, they didn't go to the AIAW National Championship or the NWIT.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-21)

In the 1979–80 season, the Longhorns continued to improve, making their first ever appearance in the [AIAW Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIAW_women's_basketball_tournament "AIAW women's basketball tournament") which was the national championship tournament until 1981. They would go again, in 1981 and 1982 (at which time it was an alternative to the NCAA Championship). Texas went 33-4 that season and finished ranked #7. In the post-season they finished 2nd to Stephen F. Austin in the Texas AIAW and lost to #9 Maryland in the 2nd Round of the AIAW Championship after beating #20 Mercer.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-22) Conradt received the AIAW National Coach of the Year award, the first of 4 National Coach of the year awards she would win.

In 1980–81, Texas went 28-8 and won its first Texas AIAW tournament championship in school history. It also won the first "Southwest Conference Tournament," a mid-season tournament in Houston made of Southwest Conference teams.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-23) It went back to the AIAW tournament and lost in the first round at home against Illinois State to finish the season ranked #16.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-24)

In 1981–82, Texas again won the "Southwest Conference Tournament" and the Texas AIAW as well as the AIAW Region 4 tournament. Most of the top teams went to the brand new NCAA Championship game in the postseason; but Texas, Rutgers and Villanova were the only top 20 teams to choose the [AIAW tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_AIAW_National_Division_I_Basketball_Championship "1982 AIAW National Division I Basketball Championship"), which was held at the same time, instead. After beating Central Missouri State, Wisconsin and Wayland Baptist, Texas played in their first National Championship game where they lost to [Rutgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutgers_Scarlet_Knights_women's_basketball "Rutgers Scarlet Knights women's basketball") 83-77 and finished the season ranked #5.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-25)

#### Southwest Conference

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Southwest Conference")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/1986_natl_champ_tower_s001.jpg/250px-1986_natl_champ_tower_s001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1986_natl_champ_tower_s001.jpg)

The Texas team, in front of the main tower, lit up with #1

By the time Southwest Conference play began in 1983, Texas was the conference's dominant team. They entered the tournament with an 8–0 conference record and a #3 ranking. They won the tournament with a combined margin of 101 points and earned the conference's automatic bid to the NCAA basketball tournament. They hosted their first game that year, a first round win over Louisville, and then advanced to the Regional Championship which they lost to #1 seed and eventual runner-up Louisiana Tech. For the season, Conradt was named conference and [WBCA National Coach of the Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WBCA_National_Coach_of_the_Year_Award "WBCA National Coach of the Year Award") of the year, her first time winning either award and [Annette Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annette_Smith "Annette Smith") was named the Conference player of the year.

In 1984 and 1985 Texas again went undefeated in Southwest Conference play, won the conference tournament and went into the NCAA Tournament with the No. 1 ranking according in the AP poll,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-1984_AP-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-1985_AP-27) but failed to win the national championship in either year. In 1984, after going 30-2 and despite being the #1 ranked team they were a #2 seed in the tournament. They hosted Drake in the first round but after suffering knee injuries to five key players, including injuries to center Annette Smith so severe she was in rehabilitation for well over a year, they lost to Louisiana Tech in the Regional Championships on Tech's home court again.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-SI-28) In 1985, they went 28–3, but were upset by a buzzer beating shot by [Western Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Kentucky_Lady_Toppers_basketball "Western Kentucky Lady Toppers basketball"), and lost 92–90 in the Mideast Regional semifinals.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-SI-28) Conradt again won conference coach of the year honors in each season while Smith was Conference Player of the Year in 1984 and [Fran Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran_Harris "Fran Harris") was in 1985.

1986 would end differently. They started the season by winning the Texas Classic and the Orange Bowl Invitational pre-season tournaments. Then they again went undefeated in conference play, won the Southwest Conference championship and finished the season ranked #1,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-1986_AP-29) but instead of making an early exit, they went on to win every single game, achieving a record of 34–0 and won the National Championship. They posted the first undefeated season in women's basketball during the NCAA era (since 1982), the first in NCAA basketball since the 1975-76 Indiana Hoosiers and one of 10 undefeated season in women's college basketball overall as of 2025.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-30) Conradt won her 4th straight conference coach of the year award, and her second, and final, WBCA National Coach of the Year Award (her 3rd time winning National Coach of the Year). Meanwhile, for the 4th time in a row a Longhorn, [Kamie Ethridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamie_Ethridge "Kamie Ethridge"), was named as Conference Player of the Year. Ethridge was also an All-American (again) who won the Conference Female Athlete of the Year of the award, the Wade Trophy for best upperclass women's basketball player in the NCAA, the Honda Sports Award for the nation's best collegiate female basketball athlete and the [Honda-Broderick Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honda-Broderick_Cup "Honda-Broderick Cup") for Collegiate Woman Athlete of the Year (the only Longhorn to ever win the award).

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Smith_conradt_trophy_s86001usc.jpg/250px-Smith_conradt_trophy_s86001usc.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Smith_conradt_trophy_s86001usc.jpg)

Annette Smith and Jody Conradt with the National Championship trophy

The 1986–87 season saw the previous year's NCAA Final Four MVP [Clarissa Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarissa_Davis "Clarissa Davis") and 1988 Olympian [Andrea Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Lloyd-Curry "Andrea Lloyd-Curry") lead the team to their 5th straight undefeated Southwest Conference season and conference championship and then back to the Final Four, hosted in Austin. The Lady Longhorns fell in the national semifinals, 70–67, to nemesis Louisiana Tech. Conradt won Conference Coach of the year for the 5th time in a row, Lloyd was named conference Player of the Year and Davis was named the Naismith National Player of the Year.

Davis suffered a knee injury in the 1987–88 season, limiting her to action in just nine games,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-31) but behind the play of Southwest Conference Player of the Year Yulonda Wimbish the team rallied for another undefeated Southwest Conference championship season, SWC Tournament title, and No. 1 national seed in the NCAAs. Again, it was Louisiana Tech that ended the Longhorns' season — in Austin — with an 83–80 win in the Elite Eight.

Two recruiting arrivals in the fall of 1988 and fall of 1989 brought hopes that Texas would return to the Final Four: Catarina Pollini, a highly touted, 6-foot-5 European standout, and [Vicki Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicki_Hall "Vicki Hall"), the Gatorade National Player of the Year, joining the program before the 1988–89 season.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-2021-22_Postseason_Media_Guide-3) Pollini, a junior transfer, suffered a knee injury and missed 12 games in 1988–89 before returning to limited action. At that time, an obscure NCAA rule revealed that if she played past her March 16 birthday that season, it would be considered an additional year of eligibility. Opting to help Davis in her senior season, the team won the Southwest Conference Championship again and, as a #2 seed, reached the Elite Eight in the Austin Regional in 1989 where it fell to Maryland 79–71. Davis became the most decorated player in school history winning several National Player of the Year awards, including the Naismith Trophy, Wade Trophy and player of the year awards for the WBCA and USBWA and was named an All-American again.

In the fall of 1989, the state of Texas' top recruit in years, [Sheryl Swoopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheryl_Swoopes "Sheryl Swoopes") arrived on campus, only to leave due to homesickness before classes started. Swoopes would go on to lead Texas Tech to the 1993 NCAA Championship as Final Four MVP and Naismith College Player of the Year. As for Hall, she earned SWC Freshman of the Year honors in 1989–90 and was Texas' leading scorer the next season as Texas managed a 15-1 finish in Southwest Conference play—including a road loss to Arkansas that ended a streak of 132 conference wins. The Longhorns beat Texas Tech in the SWC Tournament championship game to win their 8th straight championship and, as a #3 seed, they again made it the Elite Eight where they lost to #1 seed Louisiana Tech in Austin 71–57.

In the 1990–91 season, Texas' dominance of the Southwest Conference came to an end. Texas lost two games during the season and finished 2nd in the regular season standings behind Arkansas. During the conference championship they failed to make the championship game after being upset by Swoopes and Texas Tech. Seeded #7 and playing at home, they were upset by [Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamar_Lady_Cardinals_basketball "Lamar Lady Cardinals basketball") in the first round of the [1991 NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "1991 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"). It was their worst performance in the Southwest Conference and NCAA Tournament since both had begun.

Against Missouri State in the opening game of the 1991–92 season, Hall tore her left ACL.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-32) Texas finished 11–3 in conference play (Arkansas had departed for the SEC) and fell to Texas Tech in the SWC Tournament championship game. The Longhorns' opening game in the NCAA Tournament's round of 32, where they were a #4 seed, saw them fall to UCLA 72–71.

In the 1992–93 season Texas again finished 2nd in the SWC regular season and was runner up in the tournament, finishing behind eventual National Champion Texas Tech in both. They were a #3 seed in the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "1993 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"), but for the 6th time in 11 years their tournament ended with a loss to Louisiana Tech, this time being upset by the #6 seed.

In 1993-94 the Longhorns finished in 3rd in the regular season, the first time they were not in the top 2 since Southwest Conference play started. But in the [tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Southwest_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "1994 Southwest Conference women's basketball tournament") they upset #2 seed Texas A&M and #1 seed Texas Tech to win the tournament. It was the Longhorns last Southwest Conference Championship. They were a #5 seed in the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "1994 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") and lost to #4 Seton Hall in the 2nd Round.

The 1994–95 season was a low-point for Texas. It was the team's first ever season with a losing record. Texas went 12–16, the worst record by a Conradt-coached team ever, and failed to make it to a post-season tournament for the first time ever. They pulled off an upset of Texas A&M in the [conference tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Southwest_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "1995 Southwest Conference women's basketball tournament"), but then lost to #2 seed SMU in the semifinals.

the 1995–96 season, the last of the Southwest Conference, was a bounce back for Texas. They won the Southwest Conference's regular season title and were the #1 seed in the [conference tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Southwest_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "1996 Southwest Conference women's basketball tournament"), but they were upset by Texas A&M in the 2nd round. They lost to #4 seed Kansas in the 2nd round of the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "1996 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"). Conradt was named Southwest Conference Coach of the year for a record 6th time.

#### Big 12 Conference

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Big 12 Conference")]

In 1996, Texas moved to the Big 12. In their first season in the Big 12 (1996–97), Texas finished the regular season as the conference runner-up and ranked #14 heading into the Big 12 Tournament where they were upset by 3rd seed Colorado. Texas hosted their first two-round games as the #3 Seed in the tournament, but made a 2nd round exit after being upset by 6th seed Notre Dame.

1997-98 was another down year for the Horns. They finished 7th in the Big 12, were upset by #10 seed A&M in the first round of the conference tournament and failed to make the post-season for only the 2nd time.

In 1998–99, Texas improved over the prior year, finishing 4th in the Big 12. But they were upset by 5th seed Nebraska in the 2nd round of the [Big 12 Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "1999 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") and lost to Auburn in the 1st round of the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "1999 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament").

1999-2000 was a mixed bag of a season powered by All-American [Edwina Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwina_Brown "Edwina Brown"). They finished 6th in the Big 12, but after upsets of #3 seed Oklahoma and #2 seed Texas Tech they made it to the [Conference Championship game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2000 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") where they lost to #1 seed Iowa State. Brown was named the tournament's Most Outstanding Player. But at the [NCAA Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2000 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") they again made an early exit after an upset loss to St. Joseph's. Brown won the [Wade Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wade_Trophy "Wade Trophy") as the best upperclass women's basketball player in NCAA Division 1, making Texas the second school to win three awards after Louisiana Tech.

In 2000–01, Texas continued to be in the middle of the conference. They finished 7th in the regular season, were eliminated by #2 seed Texas Tech in the 2nd round of the [conference tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2001 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") and was upset by Saint Mary's in the first round of the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2001 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament").

Texas finished the 2001–02 season ranked at #14 and in 5th place in the Big 12. They made a first-round exit from the [conference tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2002 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") after being upset by 12th seed Kansas, but made a run in the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2002 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") where they lost to Duke in the Sweet 16. It was the Longhorns first trip to the Sweet 16 since 1990.

[2002-03](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002%E2%80%9303_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team "2002–03 Texas Longhorns women's basketball team") represented the last, best year of Conradt's run. Behind the play of 3rd Team All-American Stacy Stephens, Texas won both its first Big 12 regular season Championship and its first [Big 12 Conference Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2003 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") and finished the season ranked #5. They entered the NCAA Tournament as a #2 seed and upset #1 seed LSU to get to its first Final Four since 1987. They lost in the Final Four to eventual champion UConn in a close 71–69 loss that Texas led by as much as 9 at one point and as late as the last 2:02.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-33) Conradt was named Big 12 Coach of the year for the first time.

Conradt won her last conference coach of the year award for the 2003–2004 season which started with an upset victory over then #2 Duke at the tip-off classic. That year Texas, powered by Big 12 Conference Freshman of the Year Tiffany Jackson and 2nd Team All-American Stacy Stephens, tied for the regular season conference championship and was upset by Oklahoma in the [Big 12 Conference Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2004 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") championship. At the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2004 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"), Texas was a #1 seed and Conradt led the team to the Sweet 16, where the Longhorns were upset by LSU, for the last time during her career.

Conradt's last NCAA tournament appearance came at the end of the 2004–2005 season. The Longhorns finished 2nd in the Big 12 regular season and were upset by Kansas State in the conference semifinals. In the tournament, the Longhorns were a #3 seed but were knocked out early by #6 Georgia.

In Conradt's penultimate season, the team suffered through only the 3rd losing season in school history. In 2005-06 they finished 8th in the Big 12 and ended the season by being upset by Iowa State in the opening round of the [Big 12 Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2006 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament").

In Conradt's final season, the team improved only slightly over their 2005-06 performance, despite having the #1 recruiting class in the country. The Longhorns finished with a winning record and in 7th place in the conference. They made it to the 2nd round of the [conference tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2007 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") where they were beat by #2 seed Oklahoma. In the first-round game, Conradt recorded her 900th career win. A few days later, they were not invited to any of the post-season tournaments marking the first and only time in school history, that Texas sat out the post-season for 2 years in a row. A few days after the tournament selections were announced, Conradt retired from coaching and took a job as special assistant to the Women's Athletic Director.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-34)

### Gail Goestenkors era (2007–2012)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Gail Goestenkors era (2007–2012)")]

Within a month of Conradt's retirement, the Longhorns hired Duke basketball coach [Gail Goestenkors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gail_Goestenkors "Gail Goestenkors") as the new head coach.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-35) She led the Longhorns to five straight NCAA tournaments, while also serving as Assistant Coach of the gold medal-winning Olympic basketball team, but quit in 2012 citing fatigue.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-36)

After a 22-13 debut season, she led the Longhorns to an upset of Baylor in the [2008 Big 12 Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2008 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") before losing to Oklahoma State in the semi-finals and then in the 2nd Round of the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2008 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") to #1 seed UConn. The first round win over Minnesota was the only NCAA tournament win during her 5 years at Texas.

In 2008–09, Texas went 21-12 and finished ranked #25 in the AP Poll and 6th in the Big 12. They were beat by Iowa State in the 2nd Round of the [Big 12 Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2009 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") and then upset by #11 seed Mississippi State in the opening round of the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2009 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament").

The 2009–10 season was the best of the Goestenkors era. Texas tied for 4th in the Big 12 and finished the season ranked #17/#25.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-37) They made it to the 2nd Round of the [Big 12 Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2010 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") but were then upset by San Diego State, at home, in the first round of the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2010 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament").

Goestenkors final two seasons were practically carbon copies. In each year, Texas finished 7th in the Big 12, was a #9 seed in the NCAA tournament and lost in the first round. The only difference was in 2011 they won their first game in the [Big 12 tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2011 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") to reach the quarterfinals.

Immediately after the 2012 season ended Goestenkors resigned, saying she was tired and needed to step away from basketball. She had two years left on her contract. She was 102–64 at Texas.

### Karen Aston era (2012-2020)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Karen Aston era (2012-2020)")]

The Karen Aston era at Texas seemed to get off to a good start when Texas beat #14 St. John's in their first game of the 2012–13 season, but it was all downhill from there. The Longhorns went on to post a 12–18 record, for the worst winning percentage in school history. They finished tied for 8th in the Big 12 and then lost to Kansas State in the first round of the [conference tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2013 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament").

Texas greatly improved in the 2013–14 season. They won 22 games, finished 3rd in the conference and made it the [conference tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2014 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") semi-finals where they lost to regular season conference runner-up West Virginia. They then advanced to the 2nd Round of the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2014 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") for the first time in 6 years, where they lost a close one to #4 seed Maryland.

The 2014-15 Longhorns again showed improvement over the prior year in what was arguably their best season in a decade. Winning 24 games they again finished 3rd in the conference but this time they pulled off an upset over #2 Oklahoma to advance to the [Tournament Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2015 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") game where they lost to #1 seed Baylor. A #5 seed in the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2015 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"), they survived a scare by Western Kentucky and then upset California to advance to the Sweet 16 for the first time since 2004. They lost to eventual national champion UConn and finished the season ranked #22.

Texas improved again in 2015-16 for their best season under coach Aston. They won 31 games, the most since 1987-88 and posted their best winning percentage since then as well. They came in 2nd in the Big 12 in the regular season, their best conference finish since 2004–05, and they were again the runner-up in the [tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2016 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") to Baylor. After easy wins in the first two rounds of the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2016 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") over Alabama State and Missouri, Texas had to mount a 10-point come-from behind victory over #3 Seed UCLA to get to the Elite 8 for the first time since 2002–03. In the Elite 8 they were beaten by eventual national champion UConn, for the 2nd year in a row, and finished the season ranked #7.

In 2016-17 the Longhorns won 25 games and again finished in 2nd place in the Big 12, but they did not get a rematch with Baylor as they were upset by eventual champion West Virginia in the [Conference Tournament Semifinals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2017 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament"). They made it the [Sweet 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2017 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") for the 3rd year in a row, the first time they'd done that since the 2002-2004 stretch, but they couldn't get past #2 seed Stanford. They finished the season ranked #14 and Aston was named Big 12 Women's College Basketball Coach of the year and one of four finalists for the Naismith Women's College Coach of the Year award; and [Brooke McCarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooke_McCarty "Brooke McCarty") was named conference player of the year.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-24RecordBook-38)

For the 3rd straight year, the Longhorns finished 2nd to Baylor in the Big 12 - this time after winning 28 games in 2017–18. This time they did meet Baylor in the [Championship game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2018 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament"), but again they came up short. They were a #2 seed in the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2018 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") but made an early exit after being upset by #3 seed UCLA. They finished the season ranked in the top 10 in both polls for the last time under Aston, who was one of ten semifinalists for the Naismith Women's College Coach of the Year award.

In 2018-19 the Longhorns finished 3rd in the Big 12. They lost to #2 seed Iowa State in the [Conference Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2019 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") semifinals and then made another early exit from the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2019 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") went they were upset by #10 seed Indiana in the first round. They finished the season ranked #22/#24.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-24RecordBook-38)

The 2019–2020 season, shortened due to Covid, was Aston's last. Texas finished 3rd in the Conference regular season and failed to win 20 games for the first time since Aston's first season. A month after the season ended, Texas AD Chris Del Conte announced that Aston's contract would not be renewed. While she went 184–83 as the Longhorns' head coach and led Texas to 4 straight Sweet 16 appearances, her teams struggled against ranked teams, going 32–47; went 1–18 against Baylor and had several high-profile players leave.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-39)

### Vic Schaefer Era (2020-Present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Vic Schaefer Era (2020-Present)")]

Shortly after letting Aston go, Texas hired [Vic Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Schaefer "Vic Schaefer") away from Mississippi State to fill the head coaching vacancy.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-40)

#### Big 12 Conference

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Big 12 Conference")]

In his first season as head coach, Texas finished 5th in the Big 12, winning just 21 games that season, but overachieved in the tournaments. In the [Big 12 tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2021 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") they upset #4 seed Iowa State in overtime to advance to the semifinals where they, again, lost to Baylor. Due to Covid, the entire [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2021 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") was played in San Antonio, giving Texas a small home-court advantage which they utilized to beat Butler and then upset #3 seed UCLA and #2 seed Maryland. They advanced to the Elite 8 for the first time since 2016, but were sent home after being beaten easily by #1 seed South Carolina.

In 2021–22, the Longhorns finished 3rd in the Big 12 and returned to the [Big 12 Tournament Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") game for the first time since 2018. After losing to Baylor the last three times they'd met in the championship game, Texas pulled off the upset of the #1 seed and won their first conference championship of any kind since 2004, their first [conference tournament championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") since 2003 and only their 2nd ever Big 12 conference tournament championship. They were a #2 seed in the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") that year and, after advancing past Fairfiled, Utah and Ohio State, lost to #1 seed Stanford at the regional final. Texas kept it close - they were only down by 5 going into the 4th quarter - but couldn't close the gap.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-41) It was their first time making the back-to-back Elite 8 appearances since 1989–90. They finished the season ranked #6/#7, their highest ranking since 2003.

After 19 years of being also-rans, the Longhorns won a share of the Big 12 regular season championship in 2022–23, but then underperformed in tournament season. They were upset by #3 seed Iowa State in the [Big 12 Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") and were then upset by #5 seed Louisville in the 2nd round of the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"). Schaefer was named conference coach of the year for his first time at Texas.

For Texas' final season in the Big 12, 2023–24, the Longhorns won 33 games, the most since the undefeated 1985–86 season, but still did not finish first in the conference during the regular season. As a result of the temporary Big 12 Conference expansion to 14 teams, the [tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2024 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") used a ladder system with Texas earning a double-bye because they finished in the top 4. They beat #7 seed Kansas and 16th ranked Kansas State to advance to the Championship game. #1 seed Oklahoma was upset, so Texas faced #4 seed Iowa State to win its 3rd and final Big 12 women's basketball tournament championship. Texas earned a #1 seed in the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2024 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") for the first time since 2004 and advanced easily past Drexel, Alabama and Gonzaga before being upset by #3 seed NC State in the Regional Championship. They finished the season ranked #5/#7 and [Madison Booker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Booker "Madison Booker") was named Big 12 Player of the Year, Big 12 Freshman of the Year and won the [Cheryl Miller Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheryl_Miller_Award "Cheryl Miller Award").

#### Southeastern Conference

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Southeastern Conference")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Madison_Booker.jpg/250px-Madison_Booker.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Madison_Booker.jpg)

Madison Booker in 2025 game against South Carolina

The 2024–25 season was Texas' first in the SEC and they started it off by winning 35 games, tied for second most in school history and the most since 1981–82. Their record of 35-4 gave them an 89.7% winning percentage, the programs highest since 1987–88. They were the SEC regular season co-champion with #2 South Carolina, winning their 2nd conference regular season championship in 3 years. In their first SEC tournament, they were the #2 seed (after losing a coin toss) and after a double-bye they beat #7 seed Ole Miss and #3 seed LSU before losing to South Carolina 64–45 in the [championship game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_SEC_women's_basketball_tournament "2025 SEC women's basketball tournament"). They were awarded a #1 seed in the NCAA tournament, making 2024-25 their first back-to-back #1 seed seasons since 1986–87. They beat William & Mary, Illinois, Tennessee, and TCU to earn their first Final Four trip since 2003. In the Final Four they had a rematch with South Carolina, but ultimately lost again (74–57). Booker was named the SEC Player of the year and won a 2nd Cheryl Miller Award. Vic Schaefer was named SEC Couch of the year.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-2025award-42)

In the 2025–26 season, Texas went 15–0 in non-conference play, and during this stretch, they won the Players Era Festival in November with wins over #3 UCLA and #2 South Carolina. They also beat #11 North Carolina at home in the ACC-SEC Challenge and #13 Baylor at a neutral site in Fort Worth in the Sprouts Farmers Market espnW Invitational. In SEC play, the Longhorns won their first 3 games before losing back-to-back road games at #12 LSU and #2 South Carolina. They went on a 5-game winning streak before losing to #5 Vanderbilt in Nashville. After this, they won the remainder of their regular season games to finish in a tie for second place in the conference. In the SEC tournament, they defeated South Carolina 78–61 to win the tournament. They were seeded 1st in the Fort Worth 3 regional and defeated 16-seed Missouri State 87–45 in the First Round and 8-seed Oregon 100–58 in the Second Round. In the Sweet Sixteen, they beat 5-seed Kentucky 76–54 and then defeated 2-seed Michigan 77–41 in the Elite Eight. They reached the Final Four for the second year in a row and faced fellow 1-seed UCLA; the Longhorns had given the Bruins their only loss of the year when they defeated UCLA 76–65 at the Players Era Festival back in November. This time, however, UCLA got revenge and defeated Texas 51–44 to advance to the National Championship Game (which the Bruins would win 79–51 over South Carolina). Madison Booker was held to 3-23 from the field and only scored 6 points. Late in the game, with Texas down 47–44, Booker attempted to drive to the rim and score, but her shot was blocked by UCLA's Lauren Betts. Texas finished the year 35–4 and they were ranked #4 in the final polls, the same ranking as in the previous season.

## Facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Facilities")]

### Gregory Gymnasium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Gregory Gymnasium")]

Originally built in 1930, Gregory Gymnasium was named after its main advocate and planner, [Thomas Watt Gregory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Watt_Gregory "Thomas Watt Gregory"). An alumnus of the university, Gregory served on the university's Board of Regents and as [United States Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_General "United States Attorney General") (1914–19) before the gym was built.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-44) Gregory Gymnasium is located on the UT central campus, a short distance southeast of the [UT Main Building, Tower, and Main Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Building_(University_of_Texas_at_Austin) "Main Building (University of Texas at Austin)") and facing west onto Speedway Avenue, the campus's central north–south street.

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Gregory_Gym.jpg/250px-Gregory_Gym.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gregory_Gym.jpg)

Front façade of Gregory Gymnasium

The Texas women's basketball team played home games in the Gregory Gymnasium annex in the 1972–73 season and then in the Gymnasium itself beginning with the 1973–74 season until moving into the Special Events Center (later renamed the [Frank Erwin Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Erwin_Center "Frank Erwin Center")) for the 1977–78 season.

### Frank Erwin Center

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Frank Erwin Center")]

The Texas women's basketball team opened the [Frank Erwin Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Erwin_Center "Frank Erwin Center") on November 29, 1977, with a 67–64 victory over [Temple College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_Junior_College "Temple Junior College").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-45)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Erwin_center_2005.jpg/250px-Erwin_center_2005.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Erwin_center_2005.jpg)

The Frank Erwin Center

Built for a total cost of $34 million, the building was named for former UT alumnus and Board of Regents member Frank Erwin.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-About_the_Erwin-47) Originally known as the Special Events Center, the facility was renamed in 1981 to honor Erwin, who had died that year.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Celebrating-48) The Erwin Center was located at the southeastern corner of the UT central campus and was bounded on the west by Red River Street on the east by [Interstate 35](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_35 "Interstate 35").

A two-level layout (the lower arena and upper mezzanine) accommodated up to 16,540 spectators for basketball games. UT undertook extensive renovations of the facility from 2001 to 2003 at a cost of $55 million, adding, among other things, new and renovated seating, new video and sound systems, new lighting, and 28 suites. As part of the project, UT constructed the [Denton A. Cooley Pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denton_A._Cooley_Pavilion "Denton A. Cooley Pavilion"), a state-of-the-art practice and training facility that sits adjacent to the Erwin Center.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-About_the_Erwin-47)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Come_Early-49)

The master plan released in 2013 for the university's new [Dell Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dell_Medical_School_at_The_University_of_Texas_at_Austin "Dell Medical School at The University of Texas at Austin") indicated that the Erwin Center would be demolished in a later phase of construction within 6–15 years. The final basketball season played there was 2021–22, with the [Moody Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Center "Moody Center") opening the following spring.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Medical_District_Master_Plan-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Unveiled-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Limited-52)

### Denton A. Cooley Pavilion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Denton A. Cooley Pavilion")]

Built during the final phase of the renovation of the Erwin Center, the [Denton A. Cooley Pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denton_A._Cooley_Pavilion "Denton A. Cooley Pavilion") opened in the fall of 2003.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Come_Early-49) The two-level, 44,000-square-foot building sits adjacent to the Erwin Center and serves as a state-of-the-art practice and training facility for the Texas men's and women's basketball teams. The Pavilion is named for [Dr. Denton A. Cooley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denton_Cooley "Denton Cooley"), a UT alumnus, basketball letterman (1939–41), and pioneering heart surgeon.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-UT_Pavilion_page-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Lap-54)

The Texas men's and women's basketball teams have separate 9,000-square-foot practice court areas, each consisting of one full-court and one half-court practice area with seven basket stations. The practice facility also includes a locker room with a players' lounge, an instructional film theater, a 4,100-square-foot strength and conditioning area, an athletic training and hydrotherapy area, an academic resource and activity center, and a coaches' lounge and locker room.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-UT_Pavilion_page-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Lap-54)

The Cooley Pavilion will be demolished and replaced during the same phase of construction of the Dell Medical School as the Erwin Center.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Medical_District_Master_Plan-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Unveiled-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-Limited-52)

### Moody Center

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Moody Center")]

The $388 million [Moody Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Center "Moody Center") is a multi-purpose arena on the campus of the University of Texas. The replacement to the Frank Erwin Center was built on a former parking lot located immediately south of Mike A. Myers Soccer Stadium.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball#cite_note-55) The arena seats 10,000+ for most basketball games and can expand to 15,000+ seats for large basketball games and other events.

The **2022–23 Texas Longhorns women's basketball team** represented the [University of Texas at Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") in the [2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season"). The team was coached by [Vic Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Schaefer "Vic Schaefer") entering his third season at Texas. The Longhorns are members of the [Big 12 Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12_Conference "Big 12 Conference") and played their home games at the new [Moody Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Center "Moody Center").

This was the Longhorns' first season at the newly constructed Moody Center.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-1) Previously, Texas played at the [Frank Erwin Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Erwin_Center "Frank Erwin Center"). This was the first time the Longhorns have a new arena since 1977 when Texas moved from the [Gregory Gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_Gymnasium "Gregory Gymnasium") to the Frank Erwin Center.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-2)

## Previous season

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball_team&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Previous season")]

### Regular season

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball_team&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Regular season")]

Coming into the season, Texas had a lot of momentum going into the 2021–22 season after their Elite 8 appearance in the NCAA tournament the previous season.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-3) However, Texas lost star player [Charli Collier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charli_Collier "Charli Collier") to the [WNBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WNBA_draft "WNBA draft"), as she was the first overall pick by the [Dallas Wings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Wings "Dallas Wings").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-4) With the addition of 2 5-star athletes in [Rori Harmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rori_Harmon "Rori Harmon") and Aaliyah Moore and 2 4-star athletes in [Latasha Lattimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latasha_Lattimore "Latasha Lattimore") and Kyndall Hunter, the momentum was still high.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-5) Texas finished the 2021-22 regular season 23–6, 13–5 in [Big 12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12 "Big 12") play.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-6) The Longhorns finished 3rd in the Big 12 behind Iowa State and Baylor.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-7) 5-star recruit Rori Harmon emerged as a top freshman as she earned many accolades such as 4-time Big 12 Freshman of the Week, All-Big 12 Second Team, Big 12 All-Defensive Team, Big 12 All-Freshman Team, Big 12 Freshman of the Year, and Big 12 tournament Most Outstanding Player.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-9) Harmon also was the first freshman in Texas women’s basketball history to earn All-American Honors. The combination of younger talent with freshmen Rori Harmon and Aaliyah Moore, plus sophomore DeYona Gaston, with the older talent of seniors Joanne Allen-Taylor, Lauren Ebo, Audrey Warren, and junior three point leader Aliyah Matharu, Texas had their most success since the 2017-18 season where the Longhorns went 24–5 during the regular season.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-11)

### Big 12 tournament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball_team&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Big 12 tournament")]

Texas earned a 3-seed in the [2022 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") where they would square off against 6-seed Kansas State. Texas would go on to defeat Kansas State 72–65 to advance to the second round.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-12) In the second round, the Longhorns faced off against Iowa State. Coming into the game, Texas had swept the Cyclones during the regular season.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-14) Texas would go on to win 82–73 in overtime behind Rori Harmon’s 30-point career high performance, advancing them to the championship game against Baylor.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-15) Coming into the game, Texas was riding a 13-game losing streak to Baylor, having not defeated the Bears since the 2016–17 season.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-16) The Longhorns would go on to snap the losing streak defeating Baylor 67–58 in the championship game.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-17)

### NCAA tournament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball_team&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NCAA tournament")]

Texas entered the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") as a 2-seed where they faced off against 15-seed [Fairfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfield_Stags_women's_basketball "Fairfield Stags women's basketball"). The Longhorns would go on to defeat the Stags 70–52, advancing Texas to the round of 32.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-18) In the round of 32, Texas played against 7-seed [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Utah_Utes_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Utah Utes women's basketball team"). Texas defeated the Utes 78–56 sending them to the sweet 16 to match up with [Ohio State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_Buckeyes_women's_basketball "Ohio State Buckeyes women's basketball").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-19) Against the Buckeyes, Texas won 66–63 advance Texas to their second consecutive elite 8.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-20) In the elite 8, the Longhorns faced [Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Stanford_Cardinal_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Stanford Cardinal women's basketball team"), who they beat earlier in the regular season. However, Stanford prevailed against Texas, winning the game 59–50.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-21)
