### Story Links

**WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. (GoDeacs.com) –**Following an inclusive and intensive search process, Wake Forest director of athletics John Currie has named Megan Gebbia as the new head coach of the Demon Deacons women's basketball program.  
  
 "Coach Gebbia is a renowned relationship builder who has created a positive team culture and consistent identity for her teams on and off the court while leading American to three regular season championships and three tournament championships in nine seasons," said Currie. "Her player development skills are evidenced by three conference Players of the Year, five Patriot League Scholar Athletes of the Year and American's first ever Academic All-American. She is the perfect fit to lead our student-athletes in maximizing their potential, on and off the court."  
  
 In her 27 years in coaching, Coach Gebbia has helped her teams reach the NCAA Tournament 12 times including a Sweet Sixteen appearance as an assistant at Marist in 2007. She is American's all-time wins leader and the only head coach in program history to lead the Eagles to the NCAA Tournament. She has been named Patriot League Coach of the Year twice and has led the Eagles to five 20-plus win seasons.  
  
 "I am pleased to welcome[Megan Gebbia](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=802)to the Demon Deacon family," said Susan R. Wente, president of Wake Forest University. "Megan will undoubtedly make a positive impact on the lives of our student-athletes and our entire University community. I want to thank director of athletics[John Currie](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=587)for leading the search process and our Board of Trustees who thoughtfully supported the process."  
  
 "American will always hold a special place in my heart – it is where I got my start as an assistant coach over 25 years ago, and it has been my home these last nine years. I will be forever grateful to Dr. Walker and President Burwell for their unwavering support and trust," Gebbia said. "I have had the honor and privilege to work with an incredible group of young women, and the hard work and dedication to both their craft and education as student-athletes has been nothing short of inspiring. We have built a championship tradition at American University, and I cannot wait to see that tradition continued in the years to come.  
  
 "What I will take and cherish the most, though, are the relationships I have formed over the last nine years." said Gebbia. "Thank you to the coaches and staff for your commitment to this program and our players – without the dedication and passion of so many, our success would not have been possible. Once an Eagle, Always an Eagle.  
  
 "With that, I'm extremely excited to join the incredible Wake Forest and Winston-Salem community and I am so thankful and appreciative of the opportunity to be the head women's basketball coach at Wake Forest University," said Gebbia. "I'm very appreciative of President Wente. and[John Currie](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=587)for giving me the opportunity to fulfill a lifelong dream to coach in the premiere conference in the country and impact the lives of young women as we help them reach their full potential on and off the floor. Wake Forest presents an opportunity to be a part of a special brand at one of the top academic institutions in the country. My highest priority will be spending time and developing relationships with our current student-athletes, alumni and the young women who will make up the future of Demon Deacons basketball."  
  
 "Our process was thorough and inclusive and attracted interest from outstanding leaders from all levels of basketball," said Currie. "To have so many championship coaches desire to be the next leader for women's basketball at Wake Forest was both flattering and validating. As a top-30 national university, with a caring and invested faculty and staff, the best on-campus basketball facilities in the country, our status as a charter member of the Atlantic Coast Conference and our home in the vibrant city of Winston-Salem and the best state in the Union, the foundation is in place to elevate this program to the Wake Forest standard of excellence."  
  
 "I appreciate both the patience of student-athletes throughout this process and the contributions of dozens of people behind the scenes to make this announcement and tomorrow's celebration possible," said Currie. "President Susan R. Wente, Ph.D., deputy AD[Lindsey Babcock](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=645), senior associate AD[Ellie Shannon](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=154), senior advisor / counsel[Pete Paukstelis](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=627), and consultant Katy Young Staudt of TurnkeyZRG and many others put in countless hours over the past two weeks to help find the right leader for our women's basketball program while also supporting our student-athletes in this time of transition."  
  
 During her time at the helm of the American women's basketball program, Gebbia accumulated a record of 160-105 (.604) including a 106-49 (.684), both the highest totals in program history. She became the all-time wins leader in 2021-22 after her fifth 20-win season with the Eagles.  
  
 A two-time Patriot League Coach of the Year, Gebbia's eight years with the Eagles have included three of the most historic seasons in program history starting with the then-program record 24-9 run during the 2014-15 season to lead the team to its first NCAA Tournament appearance. The Eagles topped that performance three years later with a 26-7 overall record to advance into the NCAA Tournament for the second time in program history.  
  
 The 23-8 season in 2021-22 ranks third in program history with all three seasons ending in trips to the NCAA Tournament.  
  
 Gebbia has mentored some of the top players in program history, including three Patriot League Players of the Year, five Patriot League Scholar-Athletes of the Year, one Patriot League Defensive Player of the Year, one CoSIDA Academic All-American First Team honoree, two CoSIDA Academic All-District selections, two ECAC Division I All-Stars, 25 All-Patriot League selections, and three NCAA Woman of the Year nominees.  
  
 Of the five Patriot League Scholar-Athletes of the Year, three were also selected as Patriot League Offensive Players of the Year with Jen Dumiak (2014-15), Emily Kinneston (2017-18) and Cecily Carl (2018-19), making American one of only two teams in league history to have players win both awards in a single season alongside Holy Cross (four from 1995-99).  
  
 In her first season in Washington, D.C., she became the winningest first-year coach in program history with a 22-10 record and the program's and Patriot League's first postseason at-large berth, facing Seton Hall in the First Round of the WNIT. A finalist for the Maggie Dixon Division I Rookie Coach of the Year award, Gebbia's squad also ranked 13th among Division I women's basketball teams with a 3.510 GPA to land in the WBCA Academic Top-25 Honor Roll.  
  
 Prior to her time at American, she helped build Marist into one of the best mid-major programs in the country. During her 10 seasons with the Red Foxes, Marist advanced to the NCAA Tournament nine times. During that stretch, they won five NCAA Tournament games, defeating Power-5 programs Georgia, Iowa State and Ohio State.  
  
 The Red Foxes, who advanced to the 2007 Sweet 16, won the MAAC regular season title every season Gebbia was on staff and won the conference tournament title nine times. Much like at American, Gebbia and the Red Foxes created an impressive home court advantage, compiling a 114-14 record (.891) in her time in Poughkeepsie, N.Y. including an 85-5 record (.944) in conference home games.  
  
 Gebbia previously was an assistant coach at Wright State for one season in 2002-03 and an assistant coach at UMBC for six seasons from 1996-02.  
  
 She got her start as an assistant coach in 1995-96 at American University.  
  
 A native of Frederick, Md., Gebbia was a key player on the 1989 Maryland 2A State Championship Middletown High School women's basketball team. As a senior she was named Co-Player of the Year by The Frederick News-Post. She played college basketball at Towson University from 1990 to 1994.

**WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. (GoDeacs.com) –**Following an inclusive and intensive search process, Wake Forest director of athletics John Currie has named Megan Gebbia as the new head coach of the Demon Deacons women's basketball program.  
  
 "Coach Gebbia is a renowned relationship builder who has created a positive team culture and consistent identity for her teams on and off the court while leading American to three regular season championships and three tournament championships in nine seasons," said Currie. "Her player development skills are evidenced by three conference Players of the Year, five Patriot League Scholar Athletes of the Year and American's first ever Academic All-American. She is the perfect fit to lead our student-athletes in maximizing their potential, on and off the court."  
  
 In her 27 years in coaching, Coach Gebbia has helped her teams reach the NCAA Tournament 12 times including a Sweet Sixteen appearance as an assistant at Marist in 2007. She is American's all-time wins leader and the only head coach in program history to lead the Eagles to the NCAA Tournament. She has been named Patriot League Coach of the Year twice and has led the Eagles to five 20-plus win seasons.  
  
 "I am pleased to welcome[Megan Gebbia](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=802)to the Demon Deacon family," said Susan R. Wente, president of Wake Forest University. "Megan will undoubtedly make a positive impact on the lives of our student-athletes and our entire University community. I want to thank director of athletics[John Currie](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=587)for leading the search process and our Board of Trustees who thoughtfully supported the process."  
  
 "American will always hold a special place in my heart – it is where I got my start as an assistant coach over 25 years ago, and it has been my home these last nine years. I will be forever grateful to Dr. Walker and President Burwell for their unwavering support and trust," Gebbia said. "I have had the honor and privilege to work with an incredible group of young women, and the hard work and dedication to both their craft and education as student-athletes has been nothing short of inspiring. We have built a championship tradition at American University, and I cannot wait to see that tradition continued in the years to come.  
  
 "What I will take and cherish the most, though, are the relationships I have formed over the last nine years." said Gebbia. "Thank you to the coaches and staff for your commitment to this program and our players – without the dedication and passion of so many, our success would not have been possible. Once an Eagle, Always an Eagle.  
  
 "With that, I'm extremely excited to join the incredible Wake Forest and Winston-Salem community and I am so thankful and appreciative of the opportunity to be the head women's basketball coach at Wake Forest University," said Gebbia. "I'm very appreciative of President Wente. and[John Currie](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=587)for giving me the opportunity to fulfill a lifelong dream to coach in the premiere conference in the country and impact the lives of young women as we help them reach their full potential on and off the floor. Wake Forest presents an opportunity to be a part of a special brand at one of the top academic institutions in the country. My highest priority will be spending time and developing relationships with our current student-athletes, alumni and the young women who will make up the future of Demon Deacons basketball."  
  
 "Our process was thorough and inclusive and attracted interest from outstanding leaders from all levels of basketball," said Currie. "To have so many championship coaches desire to be the next leader for women's basketball at Wake Forest was both flattering and validating. As a top-30 national university, with a caring and invested faculty and staff, the best on-campus basketball facilities in the country, our status as a charter member of the Atlantic Coast Conference and our home in the vibrant city of Winston-Salem and the best state in the Union, the foundation is in place to elevate this program to the Wake Forest standard of excellence."  
  
 "I appreciate both the patience of student-athletes throughout this process and the contributions of dozens of people behind the scenes to make this announcement and tomorrow's celebration possible," said Currie. "President Susan R. Wente, Ph.D., deputy AD[Lindsey Babcock](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=645), senior associate AD[Ellie Shannon](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=154), senior advisor / counsel[Pete Paukstelis](https://godeacs.com/staff.aspx?staff=627), and consultant Katy Young Staudt of TurnkeyZRG and many others put in countless hours over the past two weeks to help find the right leader for our women's basketball program while also supporting our student-athletes in this time of transition."  
  
 During her time at the helm of the American women's basketball program, Gebbia accumulated a record of 160-105 (.604) including a 106-49 (.684), both the highest totals in program history. She became the all-time wins leader in 2021-22 after her fifth 20-win season with the Eagles.  
  
 A two-time Patriot League Coach of the Year, Gebbia's eight years with the Eagles have included three of the most historic seasons in program history starting with the then-program record 24-9 run during the 2014-15 season to lead the team to its first NCAA Tournament appearance. The Eagles topped that performance three years later with a 26-7 overall record to advance into the NCAA Tournament for the second time in program history.  
  
 The 23-8 season in 2021-22 ranks third in program history with all three seasons ending in trips to the NCAA Tournament.  
  
 Gebbia has mentored some of the top players in program history, including three Patriot League Players of the Year, five Patriot League Scholar-Athletes of the Year, one Patriot League Defensive Player of the Year, one CoSIDA Academic All-American First Team honoree, two CoSIDA Academic All-District selections, two ECAC Division I All-Stars, 25 All-Patriot League selections, and three NCAA Woman of the Year nominees.  
  
 Of the five Patriot League Scholar-Athletes of the Year, three were also selected as Patriot League Offensive Players of the Year with Jen Dumiak (2014-15), Emily Kinneston (2017-18) and Cecily Carl (2018-19), making American one of only two teams in league history to have players win both awards in a single season alongside Holy Cross (four from 1995-99).  
  
 In her first season in Washington, D.C., she became the winningest first-year coach in program history with a 22-10 record and the program's and Patriot League's first postseason at-large berth, facing Seton Hall in the First Round of the WNIT. A finalist for the Maggie Dixon Division I Rookie Coach of the Year award, Gebbia's squad also ranked 13th among Division I women's basketball teams with a 3.510 GPA to land in the WBCA Academic Top-25 Honor Roll.  
  
 Prior to her time at American, she helped build Marist into one of the best mid-major programs in the country. During her 10 seasons with the Red Foxes, Marist advanced to the NCAA Tournament nine times. During that stretch, they won five NCAA Tournament games, defeating Power-5 programs Georgia, Iowa State and Ohio State.  
  
 The Red Foxes, who advanced to the 2007 Sweet 16, won the MAAC regular season title every season Gebbia was on staff and won the conference tournament title nine times. Much like at American, Gebbia and the Red Foxes created an impressive home court advantage, compiling a 114-14 record (.891) in her time in Poughkeepsie, N.Y. including an 85-5 record (.944) in conference home games.  
  
 Gebbia previously was an assistant coach at Wright State for one season in 2002-03 and an assistant coach at UMBC for six seasons from 1996-02.  
  
 She got her start as an assistant coach in 1995-96 at American University.  
  
 A native of Frederick, Md., Gebbia was a key player on the 1989 Maryland 2A State Championship Middletown High School women's basketball team. As a senior she was named Co-Player of the Year by The Frederick News-Post. She played college basketball at Towson University from 1990 to 1994.

 Bio 

Joey White joined the Wake Forest women's basketball staff ahead of the 2022-23 season as the Director of Analytics and Player Personnel. In May 2026, he transitioned to the role of Assistant Coach/Analytics and Scouting Coordinator.  
  
 White's role focuses on holding on-court responsibilities of coaching, recruiting and scouting, He also manages video and analytics for both games and practices while heavily assisting in game-to-game scouting and preparation. White is also in charge of all sport software education and implementation, including maintaining the program's Hudl database, while overseeing the program's student managers and analytics interns.  
  
 During White’s first season working with the program, the Deacs tied the most since the 2011-12 season, defeated four NCAA Tournament teams including wins over two Elite Eight teams and grabbed 12 wins at home, the fourth-highest total in program history.  
  
 White came into the role proficient in Hudl Sportscode, the Synergy Sports Suite, and Fast Model Sports Suite while gaining experience at West Virginia as a video coordinator over the past season. In this role, he managed all scouting breakdown and dissemination of opponent video to WVU coaching staff in a timely manner in addition to managing a staff of volunteer student managers and practice players.  
  
 In addition the last year as a video coordinator, he also worked as the head manager during the 2020-21 season for the Mountaineer women's basketball program assisting in daily organization and execution of West Virginia women’s basketball activities, including practices, games, individual workouts, recruiting visits, road trips, etc.  
  
 Also, he managed a staff of volunteer student managers and practice players while also creating video content for the @WVUWBB Instagram account and assisted video coordinator in production of scout tapes, recruiting videos, and player highlights.  
  
 During his time in Morgantown, W.V., White earned his bachelor's degree in Journalism in 2020 with minors in Spanish and Sports Communication with honors. Additionally, he completed two master's degrees in Sports Management and Sports Coach in August 2022 from West Virginia.

 Bio 

Joey White joined the Wake Forest women's basketball staff ahead of the 2022-23 season as the Director of Analytics and Player Personnel. In May 2026, he transitioned to the role of Assistant Coach/Analytics and Scouting Coordinator.  
  
 White's role focuses on holding on-court responsibilities of coaching, recruiting and scouting, He also manages video and analytics for both games and practices while heavily assisting in game-to-game scouting and preparation. White is also in charge of all sport software education and implementation, including maintaining the program's Hudl database, while overseeing the program's student managers and analytics interns.  
  
 During White’s first season working with the program, the Deacs tied the most since the 2011-12 season, defeated four NCAA Tournament teams including wins over two Elite Eight teams and grabbed 12 wins at home, the fourth-highest total in program history.  
  
 White came into the role proficient in Hudl Sportscode, the Synergy Sports Suite, and Fast Model Sports Suite while gaining experience at West Virginia as a video coordinator over the past season. In this role, he managed all scouting breakdown and dissemination of opponent video to WVU coaching staff in a timely manner in addition to managing a staff of volunteer student managers and practice players.  
  
 In addition the last year as a video coordinator, he also worked as the head manager during the 2020-21 season for the Mountaineer women's basketball program assisting in daily organization and execution of West Virginia women’s basketball activities, including practices, games, individual workouts, recruiting visits, road trips, etc.  
  
 Also, he managed a staff of volunteer student managers and practice players while also creating video content for the @WVUWBB Instagram account and assisted video coordinator in production of scout tapes, recruiting videos, and player highlights.  
  
 During his time in Morgantown, W.V., White earned his bachelor's degree in Journalism in 2020 with minors in Spanish and Sports Communication with honors. Additionally, he completed two master's degrees in Sports Management and Sports Coach in August 2022 from West Virginia.

The **2022–23 Wake Forest Demon Deacons women's basketball team** represented [Wake Forest University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Forest_University "Wake Forest University") during the [2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season"). The Demon Deacons were led by first-year head coach Megan Gebbia, competed as members of the [Atlantic Coast Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Coast_Conference "Atlantic Coast Conference") and played their home games at the [Lawrence Joel Veterans Memorial Coliseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Joel_Veterans_Memorial_Coliseum "Lawrence Joel Veterans Memorial Coliseum").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Wake_Forest_Demon_Deacons_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Wake_Forest_Demon_Deacons_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Wake_Forest_Demon_Deacons_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-3)

Prior to the season, Wake Forest fired head coach [Jen Hoover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jen_Hoover "Jen Hoover") after ten seasons.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Wake_Forest_Demon_Deacons_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-4)Megan Gebbia was announced as the new head coach on May 26, 2022.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Wake_Forest_Demon_Deacons_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-5)

The Demon Deacons finished the season 17–17 overall and 5–13 in [ACC play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Atlantic_Coast_Conference_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 Atlantic Coast Conference women's basketball season") to finish in a tie for eleventh place. As the twelfth seed in the [ACC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 ACC women's basketball tournament"), they defeated thirteenth seed [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Virginia_Cavaliers_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Virginia Cavaliers women's basketball team") in the First Round and fifth seed [Florida State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Florida_State_Seminoles_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Florida State Seminoles women's basketball team") in the Second Round before losing to fourth seed [Louisville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Louisville_Cardinals_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Louisville Cardinals women's basketball team") in the Quarterfinals. They received an at-large bid to the [WNIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Women's_National_Invitation_Tournament "2023 Women's National Invitation Tournament"). They defeated [Morgan State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_State_Bears_women's_basketball "Morgan State Bears women's basketball") in the First Round before losing to [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Florida_Gators_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Florida Gators women's basketball team") in the Second Round to end their season.

The **2022–23 Wake Forest Demon Deacons women's basketball team** represented [Wake Forest University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Forest_University "Wake Forest University") during the [2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season"). The Demon Deacons were led by first-year head coach Megan Gebbia, competed as members of the [Atlantic Coast Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Coast_Conference "Atlantic Coast Conference") and played their home games at the [Lawrence Joel Veterans Memorial Coliseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Joel_Veterans_Memorial_Coliseum "Lawrence Joel Veterans Memorial Coliseum").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Wake_Forest_Demon_Deacons_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Wake_Forest_Demon_Deacons_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Wake_Forest_Demon_Deacons_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-3)

Prior to the season, Wake Forest fired head coach [Jen Hoover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jen_Hoover "Jen Hoover") after ten seasons.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Wake_Forest_Demon_Deacons_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-4)Megan Gebbia was announced as the new head coach on May 26, 2022.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Wake_Forest_Demon_Deacons_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-5)

The Demon Deacons finished the season 17–17 overall and 5–13 in [ACC play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Atlantic_Coast_Conference_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 Atlantic Coast Conference women's basketball season") to finish in a tie for eleventh place. As the twelfth seed in the [ACC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 ACC women's basketball tournament"), they defeated thirteenth seed [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Virginia_Cavaliers_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Virginia Cavaliers women's basketball team") in the First Round and fifth seed [Florida State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Florida_State_Seminoles_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Florida State Seminoles women's basketball team") in the Second Round before losing to fourth seed [Louisville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Louisville_Cardinals_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Louisville Cardinals women's basketball team") in the Quarterfinals. They received an at-large bid to the [WNIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Women's_National_Invitation_Tournament "2023 Women's National Invitation Tournament"). They defeated [Morgan State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_State_Bears_women's_basketball "Morgan State Bears women's basketball") in the First Round before losing to [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Florida_Gators_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Florida Gators women's basketball team") in the Second Round to end their season.

The 2022–23 college basketball season has come to a scintillating conclusion, crowning the LSU Tigers as DI national champions. While South Carolina saw their perfect season come to an end, two undefeated teams in Ashland and Transylvania captured DII and DIII championships, respectively.

Women’s basketball’s explosive growth shows no stopping; with this years’ tournament drawing in more viewers, fans, and media attention than ever. LSU’s win over Iowa in the national championship was broadcast on ABC for millions to access, superstars Angel Reese and Caitlin Clark gave us a show, yet I found the season’s end to be bittersweet.

There were 37 total fouls called in the title game. More than any women’s tournament game ever. There were obvious late calls, missed calls, and outright egregious calls. I would like to think, with the undeniable momentum of the sport, with millions of eyes watching, that the NCAA would want to put their best foot forward for the tournament.

To top it off, some of the Twitter discourse around the Reese-Clark trash-talking left me disappointed. Both Reese and Clark have been known to trash talk and it is part of the game. Yet of course there was charged commentary condemning Reese for the same actions Clark was applauded for.

Upon further reflection, I’m glad the sport is getting more attention. Explosive discourse around certain teams or players shows that fans really do care. The stars of our game are drawing more of the eyes and attention that they deserve. Women’s basketball continues to show it belongs in the spotlight. I hope the NCAA, officials, media, and Twitter pundits all continue to rise with the sport, treating it as the powerhouse that it is.

Personally, this college basketball season has been one to remember. Diving headfirst into my career pivot, I have taken in more basketball than in any other year. With that said, the one team that I followed more than any other was Texas Longhorns women’s basketball.

Playing their first season in the world-class Moody Center, with a talented roster, and in my hometown, I knew I’d go to as many games as I could. Although the season ended with an ugly tournament loss, it was a season the Longhorns should be proud of and applauded for.

Despite starting the season without Rori Harmon, dealing with constant injuries, and having to develop chemistry with new faces, the Longhorns finished 26–10 and captured a Big 12 regular season title. The Longhorns finished the season ranked _#11 NET, top five in two-pointers made, top five in blocks per game, and top five in offensive rebound rate_**.** Additional accomplishments include:

*   Rori Harmon — AP All-America Honorable Mention, Big 12 Defensive Player of the Year, All-Big 12 First Team, Big 12 All Defensive Team
*   Shaylee Gonzalez — Big 12 Newcomer of the Year, All-Big 12 Second Team
*   DeYona Gaston — All-Big 12 First Team
*   Amina Muhammed — Big 12 All Freshman Team
*   Vic Shaefer — Big 12 Coach of the Year

I am proud of this team’s achievements and am excited to see them continue to grow. Curious as I am, I decided to look into how this growth might happen.

I touch on insights from data, observations from games/film, and compare performance to other teams. I discuss coaching, offensive and defensive schemes, and evaluate roster potential. Some team and player data comes from HerHoopStats. Other data and film comes from Synergy Sports. Shot charts from CBB Analytics.

This is simply my humble perspective as a student of the game. There are a myriad of decisions, constraints, and strategic considerations that I am not privy to. I want to reiterate the utmost respect I have for the Texas Longhorn players and staff.

—

To begin, let’s get an idea of a potential roster for 2023–24.

The 2022–23 Texas Longhorns returned ~37% of minutes played and points scored from the season before. I believe next year’s roster will be very similar to this season. Sonya Morris is the only significant loss, key additions being 5-star recruit Madison Booker and 4-star Gisella Paul.

Incoming freshman Madison Booker looks to be a dynamic shooting forward who is tough on the glass and can handle the ball in transition. Considering her elite talent, I’d expect to see Booker garner immediate playing time. In the long run, I’d be curious to evaluate how well she grasps defensive schemes and to see the extent of her passing skills.

Incoming freshman Gisella Paul decided to forgo her senior season of high school basketball to enroll early and focus on rehabbing her torn ACL. She looks to be a big guard with a great feel for the game.

The below graphic depicts roster minute and point totals, with next seasons’ removals grayed out:

![Image 6](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:493/0*Wp9nm1Q1fP1P0meN)

_In all, we could expect Texas to return ~90% of minutes played and ~88% of points scored from 2022–23._ I’d expect this strong continuity to allow the 2023–24 team to get off to a much stronger start than this past season.

For a high-level view I pull team stats, including totals, per game, advanced metrics for the Longhorns, and an average of the same metrics for their opponents. In addition to evaluating this past season on its own, I look at trends over the past three seasons with Coach Shaefer at the helm.

Here is a chain of my thoughts from this high-level evaluation:

*   71.3 possessions/40 min is up year-over-year from 70.0 poss/40 min in 2021–22

_Despite this increased pace, assist to turnover ratio increased from .89 to 1.02_

*   Opponent three point % increased from 28.1% to 33.3%, the rate at which opponents took threes was relatively flat, but opponents made more of them
*   Team free throw rate slid from 16.3% to 15.6%, free throw % fell from 69.1% to 67.6%

_Not only has the team gotten to the line with less frequency, but they are shooting less accurately when they get there_

*   While free throw rate of 15.6% ranks in the 30th percentile, the team scored 18% of their points from the line, which ranks in the 50th percentile

_This gap between percentiles tells me the team could be forcing the issue at times, relying on foul calls instead of finding another shot_

*   Three point rate, the % of all scoring opportunities that are threes, has decreased in each of the last three seasons, from 22.9% to 18.3% to 16.8%, the latest ranking near last in the country

_I would love to see a slight increase in three point rate to instill greater upside in the Longhorn offense_

Coach Vic Shaefer shows defensive mastery and I have confidence he will always continue to do so. His teams are great at forcing turnovers, defending the paint, and forcing opponents to shoot over the top of them.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 7](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*yqILHV1PLrk_yILT)

Of Big 12 teams, Texas’ defense held opponents to the fewest average points per game, fewest PPP, and forced the highest turnover %. My only defensive worry is that giving up 33.3% from three is a bit high.

This season I noticed long closeouts, to stretch bigs in particular, were an issue. Looking into Synergy data clarifies this, showing Texas’ weakness in catch and shoot defense. They were below average in these situations, giving up 48% FG. This could boil down to poor/late closeouts or missed rotations. This might happen due to miscommunication or lack of continuity on defense.

Another small factor could be players or coaches missing details in the scouting report, knowing who the great shooters are, and treating them differently from the jump. When it’s Lior Garzon popping out or Chrislyn Carr in the corner, both above 40% shooters from three, you cannot afford to miss an assignment. These are players you don’t help off of, and that you chase off the arc.

—

Offensively, Coach Shaefer runs a dribble drive motion offense utilizing many cross-court through cuts and ball reversals. They employ drag screens in transition for quick drives and dump-offs to post players. They pull bigs to the elbows in horns action, and often employ both bigs in screening actions.

Dribble penetration is the key to the motion offense, which is why a playmaker like Rori Harmon is of utmost importance. Other keys to success would include proper floor spacing, relocations, and willingness to take threes. Motion offense is the most potent with multiple ball handlers and shooters surrounding a post player or two. Even better if your shooters can handle, and your ball handlers can shoot.

Rori and Shaylee are excellent in transition and I would expect the team to continue their transition excellence. Coach Shaefer will always make an effort to establish the inside game so I expect to see bigs in spot-up and post-up situations next season. I love the way Coach Shaefer works to get the ball to his post players in a myriad of ways. This particular set caught my eye:

I also noticed some patterns that hurt the team offensively. They relied too heavily on tough shotmaking by Sonya Morris to supplement their inside game. Rori’s shooting inconsistencies allowed defenses to key in on other threats. Finally, post players show some tunnel vision and inconsistency making plays out of the low block upon shot denial.

A lot of this has to do with team continuity and getting players to gel. Being a defense-first team, I’d assume Coach Shaefer focuses on teaching his defensive schemes to new players. You can’t get too fancy with an offensive system early on, as players need to show they can defend. However, the offensive system itself is one that could be optimized as the season goes on.

Offensive possessions ended with a spot-up 21.5% of the time, Texas scored 0.768 PPP on spot-ups, which is average. _Interestingly they show excellent potential off screens, scoring 1.04 PPP, but they only ran this action for 5.6% of their possessions._

I’d explore cuts and off screen action as ways to further diversify the offense. I’d hope to address the occasional struggle of forcing the issue at times, relying on foul calls instead of finding better shots.

![Image 9](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:682/0*rHaPbA-voCiFR3Zy)

Synergy shot quality data supports this notion that the team needs higher percentage looks. _Texas took the highest quality shots 17.9% of time but their opponents, on-average, took the highest quality shots 20.7% of time._

With defense as Texas’ calling card, I figure the next stage of growth will be unlocked on the offensive end. The goal should be to strive to take higher quality shots, and to take fewer lower quality shots. Further understanding the skills and development of the players on the roster, along with a detailed look at current offensive schemes, should allow us to identify some potential areas to exploit.

Synergy Sports categorizes players into 11 different offensive roles based on data and coded film available for each player. A myriad of factors go into defining these roles and it is not an exact science, but I like the organization it can bring to evaluating players on offense.

Looking at Texas’ roster split by role we see Rori filling in as a playmaking ball handler. Shaylee and Shay fall into playmaking wings, Djak and Aaliyah are slashing wings, DeYona and Khadija are rim finishing bigs, while Taylor is a post-up big.

![Image 12](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:318/0*EiFIh0Sp8JhlLAY2)

Texas relies heavily on Rori Harmon to make plays, run offense, and defend. She is the heartbeat of this team and I have no doubt she will continue to show she is one of the best players in the country. Rori has all the tools to grow as a scorer while continuing to hold a strong assist to turnover ratio.

Shaylee Gonzalez can create as a secondary ball handler and I would love to see her further utilized in this role. As mentioned, Shaylee runs transition very well; in watching her live I was most impressed with her instincts crashing the offensive glass. While Shaylee shoots well from three, she is dynamic as well, and could be utilized in creative actions for spot-up opportunities.

With the loss of dynamic shooter Sonya Morris to the WNBA draft, this team lacks perimeter shooting. Shay Holle is a three-point ace and I wouldn’t mind if she let a few more fly. Shay is more of a spot-up shooter but freshman Madison Booker should fill in with some dynamic shooting. I am very curious to see how the coaching staff pairs her in lineups to let her go to work.

One of my favorite parts of this Texas basketball season was seeing the growth of freshman Djakalenga Mwenentanda. I could always tell Djak was locked in, absorbing and learning. As the season went along, she shined and showed great development in the opportunities she was given. I would love to see her given more opportunities to shine.

By now I have a good understanding of overall team trends and player trends. The data has revealed strengths, weaknesses, and bright spots. The final step is to turn to film and to truly understand why something is a strength or weakness.

With film we can understand the situational context that led to bright spots and can seek to replicate it. We can find ways to further utilize the skill sets on the roster by understanding how a player has success and pulling ideas that can translate.

For each player or group listed below, I note what I feel to be the most important questions to ponder with regards to developing team offensive efficiency. By no means is this exact, rather just my gut feeling.

To dig in further, I would pull situational film for each of the below groups. I would evaluate bright spots and note how each player/group can be positioned for success. Next, with a player or group profile in mind, I can comb through film of comparable players/groups. Finally, I compile ideas from comparable groups along with bright spots of the player/group in question, for a full picture of ideal offensive development.

For brevity’s sake I’ve only included a portion of this film work below, focusing on gathering ideas from comparable players that could translate well to Texas’ roster.

Rori

*   Consistency with pull-up jumpers will free up drives to the rim
*   How can we put her in positions with better attack angles?
*   How can we generate easy offense for Rori?

DeYona, Taylor, Khadija

*   As mentioned, Texas does a great job of feeding the ball to bigs in a variety of ways
*   How can we make plays when post action is denied?

Shaylee, Shay

*   In which situations does Shaylee take high quality shots?
*   Are there ways Shaylee can score with more diversity off of cuts and screens?
*   How can we identify ways to increase 3-point volume?

Djak, Aaliyah, Amina

*   While Aaliyah finishes well driving to the rim, Djak scores in more of a diverse manner
*   How can we replicate Djak’s offensive bright spots next season?
*   Where/how is Amina most comfortable offensively?

Madison

*   How does her skillset translate to this level?
*   To what extent can she handle and pass under pressure?

Again, I focused on offense throughout this analysis. It’s where I see a lot of upside, considering the talent on this team. I love Texas’ motion offense and the way they play through their bigs. By no means am I suggesting they stray away from this.

My trust in Texas’ defense is all thanks to masterful coaching from Shaefer and his staff. We should not take for granted the hustle and discipline that Texas plays with. I commend Coach Shaefer and his staff for their utmost professionalism and care for their players.

Now I’d rather not dig up old crap but I think it is important to understand what went wrong versus Louisville to end the season. Texas shot 18/45 from two, made 1 of 10 threes, made 12 of 20 free throws, grabbed 34 rebounds, 5 assists and 13 TO. Louisville shot 27/51 from two, made 3 of 13 threes, made 10 of 15 free throws, grabbed 42 rebounds, 10 assists and 10 TO.

Here were my written notes during the game:

*   Played Sonya Morris too long, miscommunications and turnovers
*   Hesitant play from bigs, unable to catch cleanly
*   Not attached to Chrislyn Carr, she shoots 43% from three and had too much space
*   Rori’s lack of shooting threat allowing their defense to key in on others
*   With Shay and Shaylee not hitting shots, bigs in foul trouble, and Rori not shooting well, the team needs a jolt out of the locker room at half
*   Djak has shown an ability to score, I’d start her coming out of half

On top of the rebounding margin and turnover margin, Texas just was not making the shots they usually make. As I digested my game notes I noticed an overlap with the issues I had noticed throughout the season; same as those I have mentioned earlier in this analysis.

While I am not sure there was much to be done that evening versus Louisville, I am optimistic about Texas’ tournament potential going forward. With defense to always hang their hats on, I believe we will see a more potent Texas offense next season.

Roster continuity going into next season will be a huge advantage. Coach Shaefer will continue to find ways to feed the ball to Jones and Gaston down low. Rori being the superstar she is, will no doubt find consistency with her jump shot.

I believe the team can continue to pursue transition scoring opportunities, perhaps with even more frequency considering Madison Booker’s skills. I would install more cuts and screening action to free up Rori, Shaylee, Aaliyah, and Djak. Finally, I’d plan to slowly ramp up three point volume; encouraging Shay and Shaylee to confidently step into more shots without hesitation.

The 2022–23 college basketball season has come to a scintillating conclusion, crowning the LSU Tigers as DI national champions. While South Carolina saw their perfect season come to an end, two undefeated teams in Ashland and Transylvania captured DII and DIII championships, respectively.

Women’s basketball’s explosive growth shows no stopping; with this years’ tournament drawing in more viewers, fans, and media attention than ever. LSU’s win over Iowa in the national championship was broadcast on ABC for millions to access, superstars Angel Reese and Caitlin Clark gave us a show, yet I found the season’s end to be bittersweet.

There were 37 total fouls called in the title game. More than any women’s tournament game ever. There were obvious late calls, missed calls, and outright egregious calls. I would like to think, with the undeniable momentum of the sport, with millions of eyes watching, that the NCAA would want to put their best foot forward for the tournament.

To top it off, some of the Twitter discourse around the Reese-Clark trash-talking left me disappointed. Both Reese and Clark have been known to trash talk and it is part of the game. Yet of course there was charged commentary condemning Reese for the same actions Clark was applauded for.

Upon further reflection, I’m glad the sport is getting more attention. Explosive discourse around certain teams or players shows that fans really do care. The stars of our game are drawing more of the eyes and attention that they deserve. Women’s basketball continues to show it belongs in the spotlight. I hope the NCAA, officials, media, and Twitter pundits all continue to rise with the sport, treating it as the powerhouse that it is.

—

Personally, this college basketball season has been one to remember. Diving headfirst into my career pivot, I have taken in more basketball than in any other year. With that said, the one team that I followed more than any other was Texas Longhorns women’s basketball.

Photo Credit: Texas Athletics

Playing their first season in the world-class Moody Center, with a talented roster, and in my hometown, I knew I’d go to as many games as I could. Although the season ended with an ugly tournament loss, it was a season the Longhorns should be proud of and applauded for.

Despite starting the season without Rori Harmon, dealing with constant injuries, and having to develop chemistry with new faces, the Longhorns finished 26–10 and captured a Big 12 regular season title. The Longhorns finished the season ranked _#11 NET, top five in two-pointers made, top five in blocks per game, and top five in offensive rebound rate_**.** Additional accomplishments include:

*   Rori Harmon — AP All-America Honorable Mention, Big 12 Defensive Player of the Year, All-Big 12 First Team, Big 12 All Defensive Team
*   Shaylee Gonzalez — Big 12 Newcomer of the Year, All-Big 12 Second Team
*   DeYona Gaston — All-Big 12 First Team
*   Amina Muhammed — Big 12 All Freshman Team
*   Vic Shaefer — Big 12 Coach of the Year

I am proud of this team’s achievements and am excited to see them continue to grow. Curious as I am, I decided to look into how this growth might happen.

I touch on insights from data, observations from games/film, and compare performance to other teams. I discuss coaching, offensive and defensive schemes, and evaluate roster potential. Some team and player data comes from HerHoopStats. Other data and film comes from Synergy Sports. Shot charts from CBB Analytics.

This is simply my humble perspective as a student of the game. There are a myriad of decisions, constraints, and strategic considerations that I am not privy to. I want to reiterate the utmost respect I have for the Texas Longhorn players and staff.

—

To begin, let’s get an idea of a potential roster for 2023–24.

The 2022–23 Texas Longhorns returned ~37% of minutes played and points scored from the season before. I believe next year’s roster will be very similar to this season. Sonya Morris is the only significant loss, key additions being 5-star recruit Madison Booker and 4-star Gisella Paul.

Incoming freshman Madison Booker looks to be a dynamic shooting forward who is tough on the glass and can handle the ball in transition. Considering her elite talent, I’d expect to see Booker garner immediate playing time. In the long run, I’d be curious to evaluate how well she grasps defensive schemes and to see the extent of her passing skills.

Incoming freshman Gisella Paul decided to forgo her senior season of high school basketball to enroll early and focus on rehabbing her torn ACL. She looks to be a big guard with a great feel for the game.

The below graphic depicts roster minute and point totals, with next seasons’ removals grayed out:

![Image 6](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:493/0*Wp9nm1Q1fP1P0meN)

_In all, we could expect Texas to return ~90% of minutes played and ~88% of points scored from 2022–23._ I’d expect this strong continuity to allow the 2023–24 team to get off to a much stronger start than this past season.

—

For a high-level view I pull team stats, including totals, per game, advanced metrics for the Longhorns, and an average of the same metrics for their opponents. In addition to evaluating this past season on its own, I look at trends over the past three seasons with Coach Shaefer at the helm.

Here is a chain of my thoughts from this high-level evaluation:

*   71.3 possessions/40 min is up year-over-year from 70.0 poss/40 min in 2021–22

_Despite this increased pace, assist to turnover ratio increased from .89 to 1.02_

*   Opponent three point % increased from 28.1% to 33.3%, the rate at which opponents took threes was relatively flat, but opponents made more of them
*   Team free throw rate slid from 16.3% to 15.6%, free throw % fell from 69.1% to 67.6%

_Not only has the team gotten to the line with less frequency, but they are shooting less accurately when they get there_

*   While free throw rate of 15.6% ranks in the 30th percentile, the team scored 18% of their points from the line, which ranks in the 50th percentile

_This gap between percentiles tells me the team could be forcing the issue at times, relying on foul calls instead of finding another shot_

*   Three point rate, the % of all scoring opportunities that are threes, has decreased in each of the last three seasons, from 22.9% to 18.3% to 16.8%, the latest ranking near last in the country

_I would love to see a slight increase in three point rate to instill greater upside in the Longhorn offense_

Coach Vic Shaefer shows defensive mastery and I have confidence he will always continue to do so. His teams are great at forcing turnovers, defending the paint, and forcing opponents to shoot over the top of them.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 7](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*yqILHV1PLrk_yILT)

Of Big 12 teams, Texas’ defense held opponents to the fewest average points per game, fewest PPP, and forced the highest turnover %. My only defensive worry is that giving up 33.3% from three is a bit high.

This season I noticed long closeouts, to stretch bigs in particular, were an issue. Looking into Synergy data clarifies this, showing Texas’ weakness in catch and shoot defense. They were below average in these situations, giving up 48% FG. This could boil down to poor/late closeouts or missed rotations. This might happen due to miscommunication or lack of continuity on defense.

Another small factor could be players or coaches missing details in the scouting report, knowing who the great shooters are, and treating them differently from the jump. When it’s Lior Garzon popping out or Chrislyn Carr in the corner, both above 40% shooters from three, you cannot afford to miss an assignment. These are players you don’t help off of, and that you chase off the arc.

—

Offensively, Coach Shaefer runs a dribble drive motion offense utilizing many cross-court through cuts and ball reversals. They employ drag screens in transition for quick drives and dump-offs to post players. They pull bigs to the elbows in horns action, and often employ both bigs in screening actions.

Dribble penetration is the key to the motion offense, which is why a playmaker like Rori Harmon is of utmost importance. Other keys to success would include proper floor spacing, relocations, and willingness to take threes. Motion offense is the most potent with multiple ball handlers and shooters surrounding a post player or two. Even better if your shooters can handle, and your ball handlers can shoot.

Rori and Shaylee are excellent in transition and I would expect the team to continue their transition excellence. Coach Shaefer will always make an effort to establish the inside game so I expect to see bigs in spot-up and post-up situations next season. I love the way Coach Shaefer works to get the ball to his post players in a myriad of ways. This particular set caught my eye:

I also noticed some patterns that hurt the team offensively. They relied too heavily on tough shotmaking by Sonya Morris to supplement their inside game. Rori’s shooting inconsistencies allowed defenses to key in on other threats. Finally, post players show some tunnel vision and inconsistency making plays out of the low block upon shot denial.

A lot of this has to do with team continuity and getting players to gel. Being a defense-first team, I’d assume Coach Shaefer focuses on teaching his defensive schemes to new players. You can’t get too fancy with an offensive system early on, as players need to show they can defend. However, the offensive system itself is one that could be optimized as the season goes on.

To further understand Texas offense, I dug into a breakdown of all offensive play types from the season.

![Image 8](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*bye2DPakDJc101o8)

Offensive possessions ended with a spot-up 21.5% of the time, Texas scored 0.768 PPP on spot-ups, which is average. _Interestingly they show excellent potential off screens, scoring 1.04 PPP, but they only ran this action for 5.6% of their possessions._

I’d explore cuts and off screen action as ways to further diversify the offense. I’d hope to address the occasional struggle of forcing the issue at times, relying on foul calls instead of finding better shots.

![Image 9](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:682/0*rHaPbA-voCiFR3Zy)

Synergy shot quality data supports this notion that the team needs higher percentage looks. _Texas took the highest quality shots 17.9% of time but their opponents, on-average, took the highest quality shots 20.7% of time._

![Image 10](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*NkeuXEn8_C20NyuO)

# Texas Women’s Basketball 2022-23 Roster Analysis

![Image 2](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/834fa67087e9d395bcdbf96e68d93f5a5fe85d2ead2c473b658823d7bdb6bb19?s=50&d=mm&r=g)

By[Matthew Postins](https://www.heartlandcollegesports.com/author/mpostins/)[](https://x.com/PostinsPostcard)[](mailto:mpostins@gmail.com)

Posted on October 13, 2022

![Image 3: NCAA Womens Basketball: Texas at Tennessee](https://www.heartlandcollegesports.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/USATSI_17254167.jpg)

ShareTweet[Share](whatsapp://send?text=Texas%20Women%E2%80%99s%20Basketball%202022-23%20Roster%20Analysis%20https://www.heartlandcollegesports.com/2022/10/13/texas-womens-basketball-2022-23-roster-analysis/)Share[Forum](https://www.heartlandcollegesports.com/members-forum/)[Email](mailto:?subject=Texas%20Women%E2%80%99s%20Basketball%202022-23%20Roster%20Analysis&BODY=I%20found%20this%20article%20interesting%20and%20thought%20of%20sharing%20it%20with%20you.%20Check%20it%20out:%20https://www.heartlandcollegesports.com/2022/10/13/texas-womens-basketball-2022-23-roster-analysis/)
Leading up to the opening of the 2022-23 Big 12 women’s basketball season Heartland College Sports will analyze each of the Big 12 women’s basketball rosters. Today it’s the Texas Longhorns.

**2021-22 Season-Ending Roster**: F Lauren Ebo, G Aliyah Matharu, G Rori Harmon, G/F Kobe King-Hawea, F Deyona Gaston, G Shay Holle, G Joanne Allen-Taylor, F Aaliyah Moore, G Kyndall Hunter, G Audrey Warren, C Femme Masudi, F Latasha Lattimore, G Anissa Gutierrez.

**No longer at Texas:**Ebo (transferred to Notre Dame), Matharu (transferred to Florida), King-Hawea (transferred to James Madison), Allen-Taylor (out of eligibility), Warren (transferred to Georgia), Lattimore (transferred to Miami (FL).

**2022-23 Season-Opening Roster**: G Shaylee Gonzalez (5-10, Sr.), G Rori Harmon (5-6, So.), G Anissa Gutierrez (5-7, Sr.), F Deyona Gaston (6-2, Jr.), G Shay Holle (6-0, Jr.), G Sonya Morris (5-10, Sr), G Jordana Codio (6-1, Fr.), Amina Muhammad (6-4, Fr.), F Khadija Faye (6-4, Jr.), G Kyndall Hunter (5-7, So.), F Aaliyah Moore (6-1, So.), G Ndjakalenga Mwenentanda (6-2, Fr.), C Femme Masudi (6-5, Jr.), F Taylor Jones (6-4, Jr.).

**How The Longhorns Are Built**

**Returning Players (7):**Harmon, Gutierrez, Gaston, Holle, Hunter, Moore, Masudi.

**Transfers (4):**Gonzalez (transferred from BYU), Morris (transferred from DePaul), Faye (transferred from Texas Tech), Jones (transferred from Oregon State).

**Freshman/Recruiting Class (3):** Codio, Muhammad, Mwenentanda.

**Potential starting lineup:**Gonzalez, Harmon, Jones, Moore, Morris.

**Why?:**If this is the lineup, it has the potential to be the most explosive in the Big 12 and, perhaps, the country. Harmon returns as the facilitator, but by the end of her freshman season, she was the straw that stirred the drink, honestly. The Big 12 Freshman of the Year and Big 12 All-Defensive selection averaged 11.4 points and 4.4 rebounds while leading the team with 180 assists and 86 steals. Moore missed time due to injury and only started nine games, but she exploded in the postseason with a 21-point game against Utah in the NCAA Tournament. She spent time playing internationally for Team USA this offseason. The other three are transfers and all were stars at their former programs. Gonzalez was the West Coast Conference Player of the Year and averaged 18.3 points, 5.9 rebounds, 4.5 assists, and 2.3 steals. Morris averaged 17.6 points last season and left DePaul No. 9 all-time in scoring. Jones averaged 12.4 points and 6.9 rebounds for Oregon State but only played nine games due to injury. The season before she averaged 12.3 points and 8.8 rebounds and led the Pac-12 in rebounding. If these three transfers play defense to coach Vic Schaefer’s standards, then good luck finding a hole in this lineup.

**The bench:**Gaston, Holle, Hunter, Faye

**Why?**Gaston and Holle both started for Texas last season. With the influx of transfers, they’ll probably move to the bench, but that’s good depth for the Longhorns. Gaston is a physical forward who can score and rebound. Holle plays defense exactly how Schaefer likes, and she has a solid outside shot. Hunter didn’t play much last year, but she was another top recruit in the same class with Harmon and Moore, and she should get more opportunities. Faye averaged 6.0 points and 5.5 rebounds in two years at Texas Tech and she should give Texas valuable minutes.

**The wild card:**Mwenentanda. It’s a loaded incoming recruiting class and Mwenentanda is a player that can make inroads to playing time thanks to her size at the guard position. But, given the talent on that roster, playing time will be hard to find, at least at the start of the season.

_**Note**: After the publication of this analysis, Schaefer said that Codio would redshirt due to injury and that Hunter was away from the team for personal reasons._

# Texas Women’s Basketball 2022-23 Roster Analysis

![Image 2](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/834fa67087e9d395bcdbf96e68d93f5a5fe85d2ead2c473b658823d7bdb6bb19?s=50&d=mm&r=g)

Leading up to the opening of the 2022-23 Big 12 women’s basketball season Heartland College Sports will analyze each of the Big 12 women’s basketball rosters. Today it’s the Texas Longhorns.

**2021-22 Season-Ending Roster**: F Lauren Ebo, G Aliyah Matharu, G Rori Harmon, G/F Kobe King-Hawea, F Deyona Gaston, G Shay Holle, G Joanne Allen-Taylor, F Aaliyah Moore, G Kyndall Hunter, G Audrey Warren, C Femme Masudi, F Latasha Lattimore, G Anissa Gutierrez.

**No longer at Texas:**Ebo (transferred to Notre Dame), Matharu (transferred to Florida), King-Hawea (transferred to James Madison), Allen-Taylor (out of eligibility), Warren (transferred to Georgia), Lattimore (transferred to Miami (FL).

**2022-23 Season-Opening Roster**: G Shaylee Gonzalez (5-10, Sr.), G Rori Harmon (5-6, So.), G Anissa Gutierrez (5-7, Sr.), F Deyona Gaston (6-2, Jr.), G Shay Holle (6-0, Jr.), G Sonya Morris (5-10, Sr), G Jordana Codio (6-1, Fr.), Amina Muhammad (6-4, Fr.), F Khadija Faye (6-4, Jr.), G Kyndall Hunter (5-7, So.), F Aaliyah Moore (6-1, So.), G Ndjakalenga Mwenentanda (6-2, Fr.), C Femme Masudi (6-5, Jr.), F Taylor Jones (6-4, Jr.).

**How The Longhorns Are Built**

**Returning Players (7):**Harmon, Gutierrez, Gaston, Holle, Hunter, Moore, Masudi.

**Transfers (4):**Gonzalez (transferred from BYU), Morris (transferred from DePaul), Faye (transferred from Texas Tech), Jones (transferred from Oregon State).

**Freshman/Recruiting Class (3):** Codio, Muhammad, Mwenentanda.

**Potential starting lineup:**Gonzalez, Harmon, Jones, Moore, Morris.

**Why?:**If this is the lineup, it has the potential to be the most explosive in the Big 12 and, perhaps, the country. Harmon returns as the facilitator, but by the end of her freshman season, she was the straw that stirred the drink, honestly. The Big 12 Freshman of the Year and Big 12 All-Defensive selection averaged 11.4 points and 4.4 rebounds while leading the team with 180 assists and 86 steals. Moore missed time due to injury and only started nine games, but she exploded in the postseason with a 21-point game against Utah in the NCAA Tournament. She spent time playing internationally for Team USA this offseason. The other three are transfers and all were stars at their former programs. Gonzalez was the West Coast Conference Player of the Year and averaged 18.3 points, 5.9 rebounds, 4.5 assists, and 2.3 steals. Morris averaged 17.6 points last season and left DePaul No. 9 all-time in scoring. Jones averaged 12.4 points and 6.9 rebounds for Oregon State but only played nine games due to injury. The season before she averaged 12.3 points and 8.8 rebounds and led the Pac-12 in rebounding. If these three transfers play defense to coach Vic Schaefer’s standards, then good luck finding a hole in this lineup.

**The bench:**Gaston, Holle, Hunter, Faye

**Why?**Gaston and Holle both started for Texas last season. With the influx of transfers, they’ll probably move to the bench, but that’s good depth for the Longhorns. Gaston is a physical forward who can score and rebound. Holle plays defense exactly how Schaefer likes, and she has a solid outside shot. Hunter didn’t play much last year, but she was another top recruit in the same class with Harmon and Moore, and she should get more opportunities. Faye averaged 6.0 points and 5.5 rebounds in two years at Texas Tech and she should give Texas valuable minutes.

**The wild card:**Mwenentanda. It’s a loaded incoming recruiting class and Mwenentanda is a player that can make inroads to playing time thanks to her size at the guard position. But, given the talent on that roster, playing time will be hard to find, at least at the start of the season.

_**Note**: After the publication of this analysis, Schaefer said that Codio would redshirt due to injury and that Hunter was away from the team for personal reasons._

The **2022–23 Texas Longhorns women's basketball team** represented the [University of Texas at Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") in the [2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season"). The team was coached by [Vic Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Schaefer "Vic Schaefer") entering his third season at Texas. The Longhorns are members of the [Big 12 Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12_Conference "Big 12 Conference") and played their home games at the new [Moody Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Center "Moody Center").

This was the Longhorns' first season at the newly constructed Moody Center.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-1) Previously, Texas played at the [Frank Erwin Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Erwin_Center "Frank Erwin Center"). This was the first time the Longhorns have a new arena since 1977 when Texas moved from the [Gregory Gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_Gymnasium "Gregory Gymnasium") to the Frank Erwin Center.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-2)

## Previous season

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball_team&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Previous season")]

### Regular season

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball_team&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Regular season")]

Coming into the season, Texas had a lot of momentum going into the 2021–22 season after their Elite 8 appearance in the NCAA tournament the previous season.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-3) However, Texas lost star player [Charli Collier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charli_Collier "Charli Collier") to the [WNBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WNBA_draft "WNBA draft"), as she was the first overall pick by the [Dallas Wings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Wings "Dallas Wings").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-4) With the addition of 2 5-star athletes in [Rori Harmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rori_Harmon "Rori Harmon") and Aaliyah Moore and 2 4-star athletes in [Latasha Lattimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latasha_Lattimore "Latasha Lattimore") and Kyndall Hunter, the momentum was still high.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-5) Texas finished the 2021-22 regular season 23–6, 13–5 in [Big 12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12 "Big 12") play.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-6) The Longhorns finished 3rd in the Big 12 behind Iowa State and Baylor.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-7) 5-star recruit Rori Harmon emerged as a top freshman as she earned many accolades such as 4-time Big 12 Freshman of the Week, All-Big 12 Second Team, Big 12 All-Defensive Team, Big 12 All-Freshman Team, Big 12 Freshman of the Year, and Big 12 tournament Most Outstanding Player.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-9) Harmon also was the first freshman in Texas women’s basketball history to earn All-American Honors. The combination of younger talent with freshmen Rori Harmon and Aaliyah Moore, plus sophomore DeYona Gaston, with the older talent of seniors Joanne Allen-Taylor, Lauren Ebo, Audrey Warren, and junior three point leader Aliyah Matharu, Texas had their most success since the 2017-18 season where the Longhorns went 24–5 during the regular season.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-11)

### Big 12 tournament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball_team&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Big 12 tournament")]

Texas earned a 3-seed in the [2022 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") where they would square off against 6-seed Kansas State. Texas would go on to defeat Kansas State 72–65 to advance to the second round.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-12) In the second round, the Longhorns faced off against Iowa State. Coming into the game, Texas had swept the Cyclones during the regular season.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-14) Texas would go on to win 82–73 in overtime behind Rori Harmon’s 30-point career high performance, advancing them to the championship game against Baylor.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-15) Coming into the game, Texas was riding a 13-game losing streak to Baylor, having not defeated the Bears since the 2016–17 season.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-16) The Longhorns would go on to snap the losing streak defeating Baylor 67–58 in the championship game.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-17)

### NCAA tournament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball_team&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NCAA tournament")]

Texas entered the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") as a 2-seed where they faced off against 15-seed [Fairfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfield_Stags_women's_basketball "Fairfield Stags women's basketball"). The Longhorns would go on to defeat the Stags 70–52, advancing Texas to the round of 32.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-18) In the round of 32, Texas played against 7-seed [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Utah_Utes_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Utah Utes women's basketball team"). Texas defeated the Utes 78–56 sending them to the sweet 16 to match up with [Ohio State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_Buckeyes_women's_basketball "Ohio State Buckeyes women's basketball").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-19) Against the Buckeyes, Texas won 66–63 advance Texas to their second consecutive elite 8.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-20) In the elite 8, the Longhorns faced [Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Stanford_Cardinal_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Stanford Cardinal women's basketball team"), who they beat earlier in the regular season. However, Stanford prevailed against Texas, winning the game 59–50.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-21)

The **2022–23 Texas Longhorns women's basketball team** represented the [University of Texas at Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") in the [2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season"). The team was coached by [Vic Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Schaefer "Vic Schaefer") entering his third season at Texas. The Longhorns are members of the [Big 12 Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12_Conference "Big 12 Conference") and played their home games at the new [Moody Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Center "Moody Center").

This was the Longhorns' first season at the newly constructed Moody Center.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-1) Previously, Texas played at the [Frank Erwin Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Erwin_Center "Frank Erwin Center"). This was the first time the Longhorns have a new arena since 1977 when Texas moved from the [Gregory Gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_Gymnasium "Gregory Gymnasium") to the Frank Erwin Center.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-2)

## Previous season

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball_team&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Previous season")]

### Regular season

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball_team&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Regular season")]

Coming into the season, Texas had a lot of momentum going into the 2021–22 season after their Elite 8 appearance in the NCAA tournament the previous season.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-3) However, Texas lost star player [Charli Collier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charli_Collier "Charli Collier") to the [WNBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WNBA_draft "WNBA draft"), as she was the first overall pick by the [Dallas Wings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Wings "Dallas Wings").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-4) With the addition of 2 5-star athletes in [Rori Harmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rori_Harmon "Rori Harmon") and Aaliyah Moore and 2 4-star athletes in [Latasha Lattimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latasha_Lattimore "Latasha Lattimore") and Kyndall Hunter, the momentum was still high.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-5) Texas finished the 2021-22 regular season 23–6, 13–5 in [Big 12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12 "Big 12") play.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-6) The Longhorns finished 3rd in the Big 12 behind Iowa State and Baylor.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-7) 5-star recruit Rori Harmon emerged as a top freshman as she earned many accolades such as 4-time Big 12 Freshman of the Week, All-Big 12 Second Team, Big 12 All-Defensive Team, Big 12 All-Freshman Team, Big 12 Freshman of the Year, and Big 12 tournament Most Outstanding Player.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-9) Harmon also was the first freshman in Texas women’s basketball history to earn All-American Honors. The combination of younger talent with freshmen Rori Harmon and Aaliyah Moore, plus sophomore DeYona Gaston, with the older talent of seniors Joanne Allen-Taylor, Lauren Ebo, Audrey Warren, and junior three point leader Aliyah Matharu, Texas had their most success since the 2017-18 season where the Longhorns went 24–5 during the regular season.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-11)

### Big 12 tournament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women%27s_basketball_team&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Big 12 tournament")]

Texas earned a 3-seed in the [2022 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Big_12_Conference_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 Big 12 Conference women's basketball tournament") where they would square off against 6-seed Kansas State. Texas would go on to defeat Kansas State 72–65 to advance to the second round.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-12) In the second round, the Longhorns faced off against Iowa State. Coming into the game, Texas had swept the Cyclones during the regular season.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-14) Texas would go on to win 82–73 in overtime behind Rori Harmon’s 30-point career high performance, advancing them to the championship game against Baylor.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-15) Coming into the game, Texas was riding a 13-game losing streak to Baylor, having not defeated the Bears since the 2016–17 season.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-16) The Longhorns would go on to snap the losing streak defeating Baylor 67–58 in the championship game.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Texas_Longhorns_women's_basketball_team#cite_note-17)
