# Kara Lawson

*   Position**Coach** 

**_As of Jan. 7, 2026_**

Olympic gold medalist **Kara Lawson**was named head coach of the USA Basketball Women’s National Team on Sept. 22, 2025. Lawson, the head coach of the Duke University women’s basketball team, was selected by USA Basketball’s Women’s National Team managing director Sue Bird and was approved by the USA Basketball Board of Directors.

Lawson, who was a 2008 Olympic gold medalist, most recently was the head coach of the 2025 USA Women’s AmeriCup Team, leading the team to a 7-0 record and a gold medal finish in Santiago, Chile. Her leadership in Santiago earned her the distinction of 2025 USA Basketball Coach of the Year.

Lawson previously led the inaugural U.S. Olympic 3x3 Women's Basketball Team to an 8-1 record and gold medal at the Tokyo Olympic Games, which was the debut of 3x3 as an Olympic event. In recognition of her leadership, Lawson was named the 2021 USA Basketball 3x3 Coach of the Year on Dec. 9, 2021.

Lawson returned to USA Basketball in a five-on-five coaching role with the Women's National Team, winning gold as an assistant coach at the 2024 Olympic Games. With the gold medal, the USA Women’s National Team claimed the longest Olympic gold medal streak in a traditional team sport. The USA Basketball Men’s National Team won seven straight gold medals from 1936-1968.

She was also an assistant with the National Team during the 2022 FIBA Women's World Cup, where she helped guide the team top gold, and a court coach for the 2022 USA National Team's spring minicamp in Minneapolis.

Lawson has helped USA Basketball teams to seven 3x3 gold medals since 2017, including on the women’s side at the 2020 Olympics, 2017 and 2019 FIBA 3x3 U18 World Cups and 2018 Youth Olympic Games; on the men’s side at the 2019 FIBA 3x3 U18 World Cup; and with both the U.S. men’s and women’s team at the 2019 Pan American Games.

In 2021, she also helped guide the USA 3x3 Women's National Team to a 6-0 record at the FIBA 3x3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament from May 26-30 in Graz, Austria. The USA's semifinal win at that tournament secured the USA's Olympic 3x3 berth.

Lawson began her legendary career as a athlete with USA Basketball in 1998 with the bronze-medal USA World Youth Games Team. Through her tenure as a player, Lawson captured gold medals at the 2008 Olympic Games, 2007 FIBA Americas Championship and the 2001 World University Games. Lawson is also the U.S. Olympic women's career record holder for 3-point percentage after shooting 57.1% from 3-point (8-of-14) in the 2008 Olympics.

Lawson guided USA teams to three-straight gold medals for the U18 women (2017 and 2019 FIBA 3x3 U18 World Cup and 2018 Youth Olympic Games) and the first ever title for the U18 men at the 2019 FIBA 3x3 U18 World Cup. The other two gold medals came from the 2019 U.S. 3x3 Men’s and Women’s Pan American Games Teams.

She also served as the athlete representative on the 2017-2021 USA Basketball Women's Junior National Team Committee, which selected coaches and athletes for USA Basketball college-aged competitions, such as the FIBA U19 World Cups FIBA Americas U18 Championships World University Games and Pan American Games.

Her impact on the women’s basketball community is evident as she was named one of the 100 most influential people in women’s college basketball as announced by Silver Waves Media in the summer of 2020.

Following an exceptional playing career, Lawson spent two years as the primary television analyst for the Washington Wizards while also broadcasting games for ESPN Radio. In addition to her role covering the Wizards for NBC Sports Washington, Lawson served as a game and studio analyst for men’s and women’s college basketball and the NBA for ESPN. On January 12, 2007, she became the first female analyst for a nationally-televised NBA game.

Hired as the Duke head coach on July 11, 2020, Lawson's first season was cut short - the Blue Devils played just four games - due to COVID concerns. In 2021-22, she guided Duke to a 17-13 mark and the second round of the Atlantic Coast Conference Tournament. In 2022-23, she led the Blue Devils to a 26-7 overall record featuring a 14-4 mark and second-place finish in ACC play, while also earning a No. 3 seed and advancing to the second round of the NCAA Tournament. Then during the 2024-25 season, she led the Blue Devils to a 29-8 record – the program’s most wins in over a decade – and an Elite Eight appearance.

Prior to Duke, Lawson in 2019-20 was an assistant coach with the Boston Celtics. She had helped Boston to a 43-21 record and into third place in the Eastern Conference prior to the stoppage of the 2019-20 NBA season due to COVID-19. Lawson was the Celtics first female coach in the franchise’s 73-year history.

In 13 WNBA seasons, Lawson averaged 9.8 points, 2.6 rebounds, and 2.5 assists in 377 career games with the Sacramento Monarchs, Connecticut Sun and Washington Mystics from 2003 to 2015. She surpassed 3,000 points, 800 rebounds and 700 assists in the WNBA. Lawson was the No. 5 overall selection by the Detroit Shock in the 2003 WNBA Draft.

A four-time All-SEC selection and two-time All-America choice at Tennessee, Lawson played for the late Pat Summitt and led the Lady Vols to three NCAA Final Four appearances during her collegiate career. Lawson appeared in 143 games, making 137 starts, and helped Tennessee to a 126-17 overall and 54-2 mark in the SEC over her four seasons. Lawson guided the Lady Vols to four straight SEC regular season and tournament crowns, as well as 2000, 2002 and 2003 NCAA Final Four appearances.

Lawson currently ranks third all-time at Tennessee in 3-point field goals made (256), second in 3-point field goal percentage (.415) and also ranks third in career free throw percentage (.847). Lawson averaged 13.6 points and 4.3 rebounds per game while closing her career ranking sixth in career points with 1,950. Lawson also was stellar in the classroom and was a 2003 CoSIDA/Verizon Academic All-America first team selection.

Lawson’s playing career has her in elite company as she is one of only three NCAA Division I women’s basketball coaches to play in a NCAA Final Four, win an Olympic Gold Medal and win a WNBA Championship (Lindsay Whalen of Minnesota and Cynthia Cooper-Dyke of Texas Southern).

In 2003, Lawson was one of seven recipients of the prestigious Torchbearer Award given by the University of Tennessee.

As a senior at West Springfield High School, she was selected the 1999 Naismith High School Player of the Year while earning All-America accolades from USA Today, Parade and the WBCA. Additionally, she was the 1998 and 1999 Gatorade Player of the Year in Virginia and led her squad to two state championships.

Lawson graduated from Tennessee in 2003 with a degree in finance. She remains a member of the Tennessee Board of Trustees.

# Duke's Kara Lawson named head coach of US women's basketball team for 2028 LA Olympics

![Image 3: Duke's Lawson named head coach of US women's basketball team](https://cdn.abcotvs.com/dip/images/17870133_karalawsonusabasketball.jpg)

Video 1Video 2

Kara Lawson was announced as the head coach for the women's team for the next four years by USA Basketball.

![Image 4: WTVD logo](https://cdn.abcotvs.net/abcotv/static/common/origins/origin-wtvd.png)

Tuesday, September 23, 2025

Share

Follow ABC11 on Google

DURHAM, N.C. (WTVD) -- [Kara Lawson](https://abc11.com/post/no-11-duke-completes-5-year-climb-kara-lawson-return-top-acc/15999028/) helped the U.S. women's basketball team win an Olympic gold medal as a player 17 years ago. Now she'll have a chance to lead it to another as the coach in the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

Lawson was announced as the head coach for the women's team for the next four years by USA Basketball on Monday.

"I mean, it's hard to put everything into words, as it's something I've been working towards. I have so much love for USA Basketball and have been so excited to serve in any capacity they ask me to," Lawson said in a phone interview. "It's the best job in the sport in our country. To lead the U.S. women's national team is such an amazing feeling. I felt a great sense of excitement and pride, and just am really grateful for the opportunity."

Naming Lawson coach was the first official move made by Sue Bird, who [started as the U.S. national team director](https://apnews.com/article/usa-basketball-olympics-bird-11d908122c676d3cfee6a9bf90770260) earlier this year. In the past, a committee would decide on the coach and roster.

"I think her resume, her experience, it all kind of speaks for itself," Bird said in a phone interview. "When you start to learn about Kara and what she's been a part of from a USA Basketball standpoint, that experience specifically made it really clear she's the right person to lead us into the next cycle."

Lawson's first chance to coach the team in a major competition will be at the World Cup next September in Germany. The Americans will play next March in a qualifier for that tournament, but that's right before the NCAA Tournament, which would make it difficult for Lawson to coach the U.S. because she also leads Duke's women's basketball team.

"Assembling a great staff for the national team is of the utmost importance," said the 44-year-old Lawson. "I'll lean on that staff a lot through that cycle. ... You have to have great coaches around you, have great players around you. We have the ability to do both, and that will be our challenge. Find the right group that will fit."

[![Image 7](https://cdn.abcotvs.com/dip/images/19836311_amoebasource.jpg) ## Deadly Brain-eating amoeba linked to Durham facility; health dept says creek lacked required permits](https://abc11.com/post/brain-eating-amoeba-killed-nc-teen-linked-water-feature-tied-man-made-creek-durham-mental-health-facility/19836230/)

In addition to the Olympic gold she won as a player at the Beijing Games, Lawson helped the U.S. win gold as an assistant coach at the 2022 World Cup and 2024 Paris Olympics and as head coach at the FIBA Women's AmeriCup in July.

"I know this from playing with her and know this from all the conversations I had with her: I'm hard-pressed to find someone who is as prepared as Kara is," Bird said.

Lawson also coached the USA Basketball 3-on-3 team to gold at the Tokyo Games, the first time that sport had been contested at an Olympics.

"Kara has been involved with USA Basketball dating back to 1998 as a high school player in the World Youth Games," USA Basketball CEO Jim Tooley said. "Her international basketball experience is extensive, including 13 gold medals. To say her journey with us has been impressive is an understatement. I'm excited to watch Kara and Sue work together to deliver success at the World Cup in Berlin next fall and at the Olympic Games in LA in 2028."

Lawson's path to coaching wasn't similar to the one many others have taken. She went from playing 13 years in the WNBA to becoming a broadcaster. From there, she spent time with the Boston Celtics as an assistant before getting the Duke job in 2020.

She led Duke to its first ACC championship under her watch last March, and the Blue Devils made a run to the Elite Eight. The team has advanced further in the NCAA tournament each of the past three seasons.

Lawson was a point guard at Tennessee and credits her time learning under Hall of Fame coach Pat Summitt as a big reason for her recent success on the sideline. Summitt was the Olympic coach in 1984 when the U.S. won gold at home in Los Angeles.

Lawson looks forward to the opportunity to coach the U.S. on its home soil in an Olympics for the first time since the 1996 Atlanta Games.

"This appointment, wherever the Olympics would be, is an incredible honor," she said. "The opportunity to lead the American side in Los Angeles in a home Olympics is more added icing on the cake. What an incredible opportunity not just for me as a coach, but the other coaches on the staff, the players that get to play in a home Olympics as well. It's a very unique opportunity that your country doesn't get very often."

# Duke's Kara Lawson named head coach of US women's basketball team for 2028 LA Olympics

![Image 3: Duke's Lawson named head coach of US women's basketball team](https://cdn.abcotvs.com/dip/images/17870133_karalawsonusabasketball.jpg)

Video 1Video 2

Kara Lawson was announced as the head coach for the women's team for the next four years by USA Basketball.

![Image 4: WTVD logo](https://cdn.abcotvs.net/abcotv/static/common/origins/origin-wtvd.png)

Tuesday, September 23, 2025

Share

Follow ABC11 on Google

DURHAM, N.C. (WTVD) -- [Kara Lawson](https://abc11.com/post/no-11-duke-completes-5-year-climb-kara-lawson-return-top-acc/15999028/) helped the U.S. women's basketball team win an Olympic gold medal as a player 17 years ago. Now she'll have a chance to lead it to another as the coach in the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

Lawson was announced as the head coach for the women's team for the next four years by USA Basketball on Monday.

"I mean, it's hard to put everything into words, as it's something I've been working towards. I have so much love for USA Basketball and have been so excited to serve in any capacity they ask me to," Lawson said in a phone interview. "It's the best job in the sport in our country. To lead the U.S. women's national team is such an amazing feeling. I felt a great sense of excitement and pride, and just am really grateful for the opportunity."

Naming Lawson coach was the first official move made by Sue Bird, who [started as the U.S. national team director](https://apnews.com/article/usa-basketball-olympics-bird-11d908122c676d3cfee6a9bf90770260) earlier this year. In the past, a committee would decide on the coach and roster.

"I think her resume, her experience, it all kind of speaks for itself," Bird said in a phone interview. "When you start to learn about Kara and what she's been a part of from a USA Basketball standpoint, that experience specifically made it really clear she's the right person to lead us into the next cycle."

Lawson's first chance to coach the team in a major competition will be at the World Cup next September in Germany. The Americans will play next March in a qualifier for that tournament, but that's right before the NCAA Tournament, which would make it difficult for Lawson to coach the U.S. because she also leads Duke's women's basketball team.

"Assembling a great staff for the national team is of the utmost importance," said the 44-year-old Lawson. "I'll lean on that staff a lot through that cycle. ... You have to have great coaches around you, have great players around you. We have the ability to do both, and that will be our challenge. Find the right group that will fit."

In addition to the Olympic gold she won as a player at the Beijing Games, Lawson helped the U.S. win gold as an assistant coach at the 2022 World Cup and 2024 Paris Olympics and as head coach at the FIBA Women's AmeriCup in July.

"I know this from playing with her and know this from all the conversations I had with her: I'm hard-pressed to find someone who is as prepared as Kara is," Bird said.

Lawson also coached the USA Basketball 3-on-3 team to gold at the Tokyo Games, the first time that sport had been contested at an Olympics.

"Kara has been involved with USA Basketball dating back to 1998 as a high school player in the World Youth Games," USA Basketball CEO Jim Tooley said. "Her international basketball experience is extensive, including 13 gold medals. To say her journey with us has been impressive is an understatement. I'm excited to watch Kara and Sue work together to deliver success at the World Cup in Berlin next fall and at the Olympic Games in LA in 2028."

Lawson's path to coaching wasn't similar to the one many others have taken. She went from playing 13 years in the WNBA to becoming a broadcaster. From there, she spent time with the Boston Celtics as an assistant before getting the Duke job in 2020.

She led Duke to its first ACC championship under her watch last March, and the Blue Devils made a run to the Elite Eight. The team has advanced further in the NCAA tournament each of the past three seasons.

Lawson was a point guard at Tennessee and credits her time learning under Hall of Fame coach Pat Summitt as a big reason for her recent success on the sideline. Summitt was the Olympic coach in 1984 when the U.S. won gold at home in Los Angeles.

Lawson looks forward to the opportunity to coach the U.S. on its home soil in an Olympics for the first time since the 1996 Atlanta Games.

"This appointment, wherever the Olympics would be, is an incredible honor," she said. "The opportunity to lead the American side in Los Angeles in a home Olympics is more added icing on the cake. What an incredible opportunity not just for me as a coach, but the other coaches on the staff, the players that get to play in a home Olympics as well. It's a very unique opportunity that your country doesn't get very often."

DURHAM, N.C. -- [Duke](https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/150/duke-blue-devils) women's basketball coach Kara Lawson on Monday hired former [Kentucky](https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/96/kentucky-wildcats) head coach Kyra Elzy as an assistant, reuniting the former [Tennessee](https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2633/tennessee-lady-volunteers) teammates on the Blue Devils' staff.

Lawson called the hiring a "big day" for Duke basketball in a statement that noted Elzy's strong national reputation in recruiting and developing players such as three-time first team All-American [Rhyne Howard](https://www.espn.com/wnba/player/_/id/4398674/rhyne-howard), the No. 1 overall selection of the 2022 WNBA draft by the [Atlanta Dream](https://www.espn.com/wnba/team/_/name/atl/atlanta-dream). The Blue Devils coach also praised Elzy's integrity, tactical skills and passion, which she believes will elevate the program.

"She is one of the best relationship-builders I've been around," Lawson said of Elzy. "She's been an elite player and coach. I look forward to pursuing championships together again."

Elzy said she is "elated beyond belief" to join Duke and added, "It is also a tremendous privilege to work with my sister and former teammate."

Lawson and Elzy were Tennessee teammates from 1999-2001 under legendary coach Pat Summitt, winning the SEC tournament in 2000 and reaching the NCAA title game before falling to UConn.

Elzy coached Kentucky to a 64-62 upset of top-seeded South Carolina to win the 2022 Southeastern Conference tournament and earn a second consecutive NCAA tournament appearance. She was 61-60 over four seasons as Wildcats coach before being fired in March after consecutive losing seasons. Elzy had also worked as a Kentucky assistant and associate coach during two stints totaling 12 years with the program.

Elzy also worked 2012-16 in the same capacities at her alma mater in addition to stops at Western Kentucky and Kansas.

# Duke women's hoops coach Kara Lawson adds Kyra Elzy to staff

*   Associated Press 

Multiple Authors

Jun 10, 2024, 12:59 PM ET

![Image 159](https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/content-reactions/share-ios-on_light.png&h=80&w=80)Share

Open Extended Reactions

DURHAM, N.C. -- [Duke](https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/150/duke-blue-devils) women's basketball coach Kara Lawson on Monday hired former [Kentucky](https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/96/kentucky-wildcats) head coach Kyra Elzy as an assistant, reuniting the former [Tennessee](https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2633/tennessee-lady-volunteers) teammates on the Blue Devils' staff.

Lawson called the hiring a "big day" for Duke basketball in a statement that noted Elzy's strong national reputation in recruiting and developing players such as three-time first team All-American [Rhyne Howard](https://www.espn.com/wnba/player/_/id/4398674/rhyne-howard), the No. 1 overall selection of the 2022 WNBA draft by the [Atlanta Dream](https://www.espn.com/wnba/team/_/name/atl/atlanta-dream). The Blue Devils coach also praised Elzy's integrity, tactical skills and passion, which she believes will elevate the program.

"She is one of the best relationship-builders I've been around," Lawson said of Elzy. "She's been an elite player and coach. I look forward to pursuing championships together again."

Elzy said she is "elated beyond belief" to join Duke and added, "It is also a tremendous privilege to work with my sister and former teammate."

Lawson and Elzy were Tennessee teammates from 1999-2001 under legendary coach Pat Summitt, winning the SEC tournament in 2000 and reaching the NCAA title game before falling to UConn.

Elzy coached Kentucky to a 64-62 upset of top-seeded South Carolina to win the 2022 Southeastern Conference tournament and earn a second consecutive NCAA tournament appearance. She was 61-60 over four seasons as Wildcats coach before being fired in March after consecutive losing seasons. Elzy had also worked as a Kentucky assistant and associate coach during two stints totaling 12 years with the program.

Elzy also worked 2012-16 in the same capacities at her alma mater in addition to stops at Western Kentucky and Kansas.

The **2022–23 Duke Blue Devils women's basketball team** represented [Duke University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_University "Duke University") during the [2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season"). The Blue Devils were led by third year head coach Kara Lawson and played their home games at [Cameron Indoor Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron_Indoor_Stadium "Cameron Indoor Stadium") in [Durham, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham,_North_Carolina "Durham, North Carolina") as members of the [Atlantic Coast Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Coast_Conference "Atlantic Coast Conference").

The Blue Devils finished the season 26–7 overall and 14–4 in [ACC play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Atlantic_Coast_Conference_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 Atlantic Coast Conference women's basketball season") to finish in a tie for second place. As the second seed in the [ACC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 ACC women's basketball tournament") they earned a bye into the Quarterfinals where they defeated rivals seventh seeded [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_North_Carolina_Tar_Heels_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 North Carolina Tar Heels women's basketball team") before falling to eventual champions and third seed [Virginia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Virginia_Tech_Hokies_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Virginia Tech Hokies women's basketball team") in the Semifinals. They received an at-large bid to the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") and were the third seed in the [Seattle 4 Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament#Seattle_Regional_4_%E2%80%93_Climate_Pledge_Arena_%E2%80%93_Seattle,_WA "2023 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"). They defeated fourteen seed [Iona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Iona_Gaels_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Iona Gaels women's basketball team") in the first round before being upset by sixth seed [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Colorado_Buffaloes_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Colorado Buffaloes women's basketball team") in the second round, in overtime, to end their season.

The **2022–23 Duke Blue Devils women's basketball team** represented [Duke University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_University "Duke University") during the [2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season"). The Blue Devils were led by third year head coach Kara Lawson and played their home games at [Cameron Indoor Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron_Indoor_Stadium "Cameron Indoor Stadium") in [Durham, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham,_North_Carolina "Durham, North Carolina") as members of the [Atlantic Coast Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Coast_Conference "Atlantic Coast Conference").

The Blue Devils finished the season 26–7 overall and 14–4 in [ACC play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Atlantic_Coast_Conference_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 Atlantic Coast Conference women's basketball season") to finish in a tie for second place. As the second seed in the [ACC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 ACC women's basketball tournament") they earned a bye into the Quarterfinals where they defeated rivals seventh seeded [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_North_Carolina_Tar_Heels_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 North Carolina Tar Heels women's basketball team") before falling to eventual champions and third seed [Virginia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Virginia_Tech_Hokies_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Virginia Tech Hokies women's basketball team") in the Semifinals. They received an at-large bid to the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") and were the third seed in the [Seattle 4 Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament#Seattle_Regional_4_%E2%80%93_Climate_Pledge_Arena_%E2%80%93_Seattle,_WA "2023 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"). They defeated fourteen seed [Iona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Iona_Gaels_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Iona Gaels women's basketball team") in the first round before being upset by sixth seed [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Colorado_Buffaloes_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Colorado Buffaloes women's basketball team") in the second round, in overtime, to end their season.

The Blue Devils finished the season 17–13 overall and 7–11 in [ACC play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Atlantic_Coast_Conference_women's_basketball_season "2021–22 Atlantic Coast Conference women's basketball season") to finish in tenth place. As the tenth seed in the [ACC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 ACC women's basketball tournament"), they defeated [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Pittsburgh_Panthers_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Pittsburgh Panthers women's basketball team") in the First Round before losing to seventh seed [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Miami_Hurricanes_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Miami Hurricanes women's basketball team") in the Second Round. They were not invited to the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") or the [WNIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Women's_National_Invitation_Tournament "2022 Women's National Invitation Tournament") despite being ranked as high as No. 15 during the regular season.

**Kara Marie Lawson** (born February 14, 1981) is an American [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") coach and former player who is the head coach for the [Duke Blue Devils women's basketball team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Blue_Devils_women's_basketball "Duke Blue Devils women's basketball") and the [U.S. women's national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_basketball_team "United States women's national basketball team"). She played professionally in the [Women's National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_National_Basketball_Association "Women's National Basketball Association") (WNBA) and has also been a basketball television analyst for [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN") and the [Washington Wizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-ESPNMedia-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-2) Lawson primarily played as a [shooting guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shooting_guard "Shooting guard"). She won a gold medal at the [2008 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), China, a championship with the Sacramento Monarchs in the [2005 WNBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_WNBA_Finals "2005 WNBA Finals"), and coached the [United States women's national 3x3 team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_3x3_team "United States women's national 3x3 team") to gold in the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:2-3) Lawson retired from the WNBA in 2015 to focus on her broadcasting career.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:0-4) She began her coaching career as an assistant coach for the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") of the [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA "NBA") in 2019.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Kara Lawson was born in [Alexandria, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria,_Virginia "Alexandria, Virginia"), to parents William and Kathleen Lawson. She has two sisters, Susan and Mary Katherine.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-usab-5)

Lawson attended [Sidwell Friends School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidwell_Friends_School "Sidwell Friends School") her freshman year, then went to [West Springfield High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Springfield_High_School_(Virginia) "West Springfield High School (Virginia)"), where she played on the girls' [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") and [soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soccer "Soccer") teams.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-past-6)

## Playing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Playing career")]

### High school

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: High school")]

Lawson was named a [WBCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Basketball_Coaches_Association "Women's Basketball Coaches Association") All-American in 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-7) Her high school record was 83–2 and won two state championships in her sophomore and senior years with a perfect 30–0 record.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-past-6) She participated in the 1999 [WBCA High School All-America Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Basketball_Coaches_Association#WBCA_High_School_All-America_Game "Women's Basketball Coaches Association"), where she scored twenty points, and earned MVP honors.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-WBCA_Box_Scores-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-WBCA_MVP-9)

### College career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: College career")]

Lawson attended the [University of Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tennessee "University of Tennessee") (UT) and played for the Lady Vols basketball team, coached by [Pat Summitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Summitt "Pat Summitt"). She enrolled in UT's College of Business, and graduated in 2003 with a degree in finance. Lawson received the [Frances Pomeroy Naismith Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Pomeroy_Naismith_Award "Frances Pomeroy Naismith Award") from the [Women's Basketball Coaches Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Basketball_Coaches_Association "Women's Basketball Coaches Association") as the best senior player under 5 ft 8 in (1.7 m).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-Frances_Pomeroy_Naismith-10) In 2018, Tennessee Governor [Bill Haslam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Haslam "Bill Haslam") named Lawson to the board of trustees of the University of Tennessee, the governing body of the UT system.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-11) In 2003, Lawson was named an Arthur Ashe Jr. Sports Scholar by _Diverse: Issues In Higher Education_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-12)

### WNBA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: WNBA")]

On April 24, 2003, Lawson was selected as the fifth overall pick by the [Detroit Shock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Shock "Detroit Shock") in the first round of the [2003 WNBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_WNBA_draft "2003 WNBA draft"). But five days later, the Shock traded Lawson to the [Sacramento Monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Monarchs "Sacramento Monarchs") in exchange for [Kedra Holland-Corn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kedra_Holland-Corn "Kedra Holland-Corn") and a 2004 second-round draft pick. Two years later, Lawson would be a key member of the Monarchs 2005 championship team.

Lawson was a free agent when the [Sacramento Monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Monarchs "Sacramento Monarchs") folded prior to the [2010 WNBA season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_WNBA_season "2010 WNBA season"), but later signed a three-year contract with the [Connecticut Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut_Sun "Connecticut Sun"). On March 12, 2014, Lawson was traded to the [Washington Mystics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Mystics "Washington Mystics") for [Alex Bentley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Bentley "Alex Bentley"), who was originally traded to Washington through the [Atlanta Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Dream "Atlanta Dream").

### US national team

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: US national team")]

Lawson was selected to be a member of the [United States national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_basketball_team "United States women's national basketball team") at the 2001 World University Games held in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). After winning the opening game easily, the USA team faced Canada and lost a close game 68–67. Needing a win to remain in medal contention, Lawson scored 25 points to help the USA team defeat Japan, and earn a spot in the quarterfinals. The USA team fell behind by 12 points against undefeated Russia, but came back to win the game by eleven points. The next game was against the unbeaten host team China, and the USA team won 89–78. The USA team won their next two games to set up the gold medal game; a rematch against the host team. China would stay close early, but the USA team prevailed and won the gold medal with a score of 87–67. Lawson was the third leading scorer on the team with 12.0 points per game and led the team in assists and steal with 16 assists and 12 steals over the course of the event.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-2001_WUG-13)

On July 10, 2008, Lawson was selected to represent the United States with the [USA women's national basketball team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_qualification "Basketball at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Women's qualification") at the [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). She helped the United States capture the gold medal, and led the team in points (15) during the gold medal game against Australia, going a perfect 5-5 from the field and 4-4 from the free throw line.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-14)

Lawson was invited to the USA Basketball Women's National Team training camp in the fall of 2009.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-National_Team-15) The team selected to play for the 2010 FIBA World Championship and the 2012 Olympics was chosen from these participants. Lawson was one of 21 finalists for the U.S. Women's Olympic Basketball Team Roster. The 20 professional women's basketball players, plus one collegiate player ([Brittney Griner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittney_Griner "Brittney Griner")), were selected by the USA Basketball Women's National Team Player Selection Committee to compete for the final roster to represent the US at the 2012 Olympics in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-Olympic_Roster_finalists-16) However, Lawson did not make the final roster.

## Broadcasting career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Broadcasting career")]

Lawson began her broadcasting career while still playing in the WNBA. She served as a studio analyst for the [Sacramento Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Kings "Sacramento Kings"), and worked her way up to working in a variety of NBA and WNBA broadcast roles for ESPN.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:0-4) On January 12, 2007, she was the first woman to work as a nationwide broadcast analyst for an NBA game, when the [New Orleans Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans_Hornets "New Orleans Hornets") took on the [Washington Wizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-ESPNMedia-1)

In 2017, Lawson was named the primary television game analyst for the Washington Wizards, replacing longtime analyst [Phil Chenier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Chenier "Phil Chenier") as full-time host. She is one of the first primary female TV analysts for an NBA team, joining [Sarah Kustok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Kustok "Sarah Kustok") of the [Brooklyn Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:0-4)

In 2021, Lawson was a commentator for [women's basketball at the 2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Basketball at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-18)

## Coaching career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Coaching career")]

On June 27, 2019, the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA) announced that Lawson would join the team as an assistant coach.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-19) During her tenure as assistant coach in the [2019–20 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%9320_Boston_Celtics_season "2019–20 Boston Celtics season"), Lawson worked closely with [Marcus Smart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Smart "Marcus Smart"), a defensive-minded point guard, as a shooting coach.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:1-22)

On July 11, 2020, it was announced that Lawson was hired as the head coach of the [Duke Blue Devils women's basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Blue_Devils_women's_basketball "Duke Blue Devils women's basketball") team.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:1-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-24) She brought on Winston Gandy, [Tia Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tia_Jackson "Tia Jackson"), and [Beth Cunningham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beth_Cunningham_(basketball) "Beth Cunningham (basketball)") as assistant coaches.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-25) Her first season as head coach lasted four games after the decision to end the season in late December 2020 due to concerns over the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").

In the 2020 Summer Olympics, Lawson coached the USA team to a gold medal in the 3x3 basketball, defeating China 18–15 in the title match.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:2-3)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-26) In February 2024, she was announced as the assistant coach for the [USA Women's Olympic Basketball Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_qualification "Basketball at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's qualification").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-27) In September 2025, it was announced that she would be the head coach of Team USA through 2028.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-28)

Lawson credits Pat Summitt with teaching her how to hold players accountable as a coach.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-29)

**Kara Marie Lawson** (born February 14, 1981) is an American [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") coach and former player who is the head coach for the [Duke Blue Devils women's basketball team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Blue_Devils_women's_basketball "Duke Blue Devils women's basketball") and the [U.S. women's national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_basketball_team "United States women's national basketball team"). She played professionally in the [Women's National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_National_Basketball_Association "Women's National Basketball Association") (WNBA) and has also been a basketball television analyst for [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN") and the [Washington Wizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-ESPNMedia-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-2) Lawson primarily played as a [shooting guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shooting_guard "Shooting guard"). She won a gold medal at the [2008 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), China, a championship with the Sacramento Monarchs in the [2005 WNBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_WNBA_Finals "2005 WNBA Finals"), and coached the [United States women's national 3x3 team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_3x3_team "United States women's national 3x3 team") to gold in the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:2-3) Lawson retired from the WNBA in 2015 to focus on her broadcasting career.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:0-4) She began her coaching career as an assistant coach for the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") of the [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA "NBA") in 2019.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Kara Lawson was born in [Alexandria, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria,_Virginia "Alexandria, Virginia"), to parents William and Kathleen Lawson. She has two sisters, Susan and Mary Katherine.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-usab-5)

Lawson attended [Sidwell Friends School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidwell_Friends_School "Sidwell Friends School") her freshman year, then went to [West Springfield High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Springfield_High_School_(Virginia) "West Springfield High School (Virginia)"), where she played on the girls' [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") and [soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soccer "Soccer") teams.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-past-6)

## Playing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Playing career")]

### High school

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: High school")]

Lawson was named a [WBCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Basketball_Coaches_Association "Women's Basketball Coaches Association") All-American in 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-7) Her high school record was 83–2 and won two state championships in her sophomore and senior years with a perfect 30–0 record.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-past-6) She participated in the 1999 [WBCA High School All-America Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Basketball_Coaches_Association#WBCA_High_School_All-America_Game "Women's Basketball Coaches Association"), where she scored twenty points, and earned MVP honors.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-WBCA_Box_Scores-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-WBCA_MVP-9)

### College career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: College career")]

Lawson attended the [University of Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tennessee "University of Tennessee") (UT) and played for the Lady Vols basketball team, coached by [Pat Summitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Summitt "Pat Summitt"). She enrolled in UT's College of Business, and graduated in 2003 with a degree in finance. Lawson received the [Frances Pomeroy Naismith Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Pomeroy_Naismith_Award "Frances Pomeroy Naismith Award") from the [Women's Basketball Coaches Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Basketball_Coaches_Association "Women's Basketball Coaches Association") as the best senior player under 5 ft 8 in (1.7 m).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-Frances_Pomeroy_Naismith-10) In 2018, Tennessee Governor [Bill Haslam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Haslam "Bill Haslam") named Lawson to the board of trustees of the University of Tennessee, the governing body of the UT system.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-11) In 2003, Lawson was named an Arthur Ashe Jr. Sports Scholar by _Diverse: Issues In Higher Education_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-12)

### WNBA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: WNBA")]

On April 24, 2003, Lawson was selected as the fifth overall pick by the [Detroit Shock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Shock "Detroit Shock") in the first round of the [2003 WNBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_WNBA_draft "2003 WNBA draft"). But five days later, the Shock traded Lawson to the [Sacramento Monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Monarchs "Sacramento Monarchs") in exchange for [Kedra Holland-Corn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kedra_Holland-Corn "Kedra Holland-Corn") and a 2004 second-round draft pick. Two years later, Lawson would be a key member of the Monarchs 2005 championship team.

Lawson was a free agent when the [Sacramento Monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Monarchs "Sacramento Monarchs") folded prior to the [2010 WNBA season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_WNBA_season "2010 WNBA season"), but later signed a three-year contract with the [Connecticut Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut_Sun "Connecticut Sun"). On March 12, 2014, Lawson was traded to the [Washington Mystics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Mystics "Washington Mystics") for [Alex Bentley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Bentley "Alex Bentley"), who was originally traded to Washington through the [Atlanta Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Dream "Atlanta Dream").

### US national team

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: US national team")]

Lawson was selected to be a member of the [United States national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_basketball_team "United States women's national basketball team") at the 2001 World University Games held in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). After winning the opening game easily, the USA team faced Canada and lost a close game 68–67. Needing a win to remain in medal contention, Lawson scored 25 points to help the USA team defeat Japan, and earn a spot in the quarterfinals. The USA team fell behind by 12 points against undefeated Russia, but came back to win the game by eleven points. The next game was against the unbeaten host team China, and the USA team won 89–78. The USA team won their next two games to set up the gold medal game; a rematch against the host team. China would stay close early, but the USA team prevailed and won the gold medal with a score of 87–67. Lawson was the third leading scorer on the team with 12.0 points per game and led the team in assists and steal with 16 assists and 12 steals over the course of the event.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-2001_WUG-13)

On July 10, 2008, Lawson was selected to represent the United States with the [USA women's national basketball team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_qualification "Basketball at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Women's qualification") at the [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). She helped the United States capture the gold medal, and led the team in points (15) during the gold medal game against Australia, going a perfect 5-5 from the field and 4-4 from the free throw line.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-14)

Lawson was invited to the USA Basketball Women's National Team training camp in the fall of 2009.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-National_Team-15) The team selected to play for the 2010 FIBA World Championship and the 2012 Olympics was chosen from these participants. Lawson was one of 21 finalists for the U.S. Women's Olympic Basketball Team Roster. The 20 professional women's basketball players, plus one collegiate player ([Brittney Griner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittney_Griner "Brittney Griner")), were selected by the USA Basketball Women's National Team Player Selection Committee to compete for the final roster to represent the US at the 2012 Olympics in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-Olympic_Roster_finalists-16) However, Lawson did not make the final roster.

## Broadcasting career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Broadcasting career")]

Lawson began her broadcasting career while still playing in the WNBA. She served as a studio analyst for the [Sacramento Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Kings "Sacramento Kings"), and worked her way up to working in a variety of NBA and WNBA broadcast roles for ESPN.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:0-4) On January 12, 2007, she was the first woman to work as a nationwide broadcast analyst for an NBA game, when the [New Orleans Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans_Hornets "New Orleans Hornets") took on the [Washington Wizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-ESPNMedia-1)

In 2017, Lawson was named the primary television game analyst for the Washington Wizards, replacing longtime analyst [Phil Chenier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Chenier "Phil Chenier") as full-time host. She is one of the first primary female TV analysts for an NBA team, joining [Sarah Kustok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Kustok "Sarah Kustok") of the [Brooklyn Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:0-4)

In 2021, Lawson was a commentator for [women's basketball at the 2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Basketball at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-18)

## Coaching career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kara_Lawson&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Coaching career")]

On June 27, 2019, the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA) announced that Lawson would join the team as an assistant coach.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-19) During her tenure as assistant coach in the [2019–20 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%9320_Boston_Celtics_season "2019–20 Boston Celtics season"), Lawson worked closely with [Marcus Smart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Smart "Marcus Smart"), a defensive-minded point guard, as a shooting coach.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:1-22)

On July 11, 2020, it was announced that Lawson was hired as the head coach of the [Duke Blue Devils women's basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Blue_Devils_women's_basketball "Duke Blue Devils women's basketball") team.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:1-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-24) She brought on Winston Gandy, [Tia Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tia_Jackson "Tia Jackson"), and [Beth Cunningham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beth_Cunningham_(basketball) "Beth Cunningham (basketball)") as assistant coaches.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-25) Her first season as head coach lasted four games after the decision to end the season in late December 2020 due to concerns over the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").

In the 2020 Summer Olympics, Lawson coached the USA team to a gold medal in the 3x3 basketball, defeating China 18–15 in the title match.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-:2-3)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-26) In February 2024, she was announced as the assistant coach for the [USA Women's Olympic Basketball Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_qualification "Basketball at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's qualification").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-27) In September 2025, it was announced that she would be the head coach of Team USA through 2028.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-28)

Lawson credits Pat Summitt with teaching her how to hold players accountable as a coach.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Lawson#cite_note-29)

## Roster Named for USA Basketball Women’s 3x3 Olympic Qualifying Team

Mon, Feb 17, 2020, 9:34 PM

/

USA Basketball

![Image 18](https://cdn.wnba.com/sites/4/2020/02/Kelsye-Cover.jpg)  

The four-member rosters today were announced for the [USA Basketball Men’s and Women’s 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament Teams](https://www.usab.com/news-events/news/2020/02/3x3-oqt-teams.aspx) that will compete in the 2020 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament March 18-22 in Bengaluru, India, where the top three finishing men’s and women’s teams will earn berths into the 2020 Tokyo Olympic Games.

Named to the USA women’s team were current WNBA players: Napheesa Collier (Minnesota Lynx/O’Fallon, Mo.), Stefanie Dolson (Chicago Sky/Port Jervis, N.Y.), Allisha Gray (Dallas Wings/Sandersville, Ga.) and Kelsey Plum (Las Vegas Aces/Poway, Calif.).

The rosters were selected by the USA Basketball 3×3 Selection Committees following Feb. 12-15 training camps in Chicago that featured 11 female and 16 male hopefuls.

“USA Basketball is grateful to all of the athletes who attended training camp and competed for a roster spot,” said Jay Demings, USA Basketball Youth & Sport Development director and member of the USA Basketball 3×3 Men’s and Women’s Selection Committees. “It was a very talented field for both the men and women, and the committees had a very difficult task in selecting these teams. In the end, we are confident in the abilities of the eight players and the strength of the teams overall. Now, it is on to the very important task of qualifying the USA for the 3×3 Olympic basketball competition in Tokyo.”

The USA women earned their spot in the FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament by virtue of their status on the FIBA 3×3 world rankings as of this past November.

As per FIBA regulations, all teams taking part in the 2020 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament must include on their rosters at least two athletes who are ranked among the federation’s top 10 FIBA 3×3 athletes.

On the women’s side Collier, Dolson and Plum also are members of the 2020 USA Basketball Women’s National Team and have won gold medals with USA Basketball.

Additionally, Collier won gold at the 2014 Youth Olympic Games, which is a 3×3 competition.

The 2020 Olympics for the first time will feature the inclusion of 3×3 basketball with eight men’s and eight women’s teams competing for gold July 25-29 in Tokyo.

On the women’s side, Russia, China, Mongolia and Romania earned Olympic bids by virtue of their top FIBA 3×3 world rankings.

Twenty men’s and 20 women’s teams will compete for three Olympic qualifying berths in the March 18-22 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournaments.

The USA women at the FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament will play in Group A with France, Germany, Uruguay and Indonesia. Group B includes Iran, Japan, Ukraine, Turkmenistan and Australia. Group C features Netherlands, Estonia, Belarus, Hungary and Sri Lanka. And, in Group D will be Italy, Taipei, Switzerland, Spain and host India.

The eighth and final Olympic 3×3 spots will be awarded based on FIBA’s universality clause, which is designed to offer an Olympic 3×3 berth to one country in the men’s and the women’s tournament who did not have a team at the 2012 or 2016 Olympic basketball tournaments. The FIBA Universality Qualifying Tournaments, which will be held in April 2020 in Budapest Hungary, will include six men’s and six women’s teams. The top men’s and women’s finishers will advance to the Olympics.

An exciting and fast-paced game, 3×3 officially was unveiled in international competition at the 2010 Youth Olympic Games and since has become a fan favorite at FIBA 3×3 World Cup events. Played on a half court with a 10-minute clock, and a 12-second shot clock, the first team to 21 points, or the team in the lead at the end of regulation, is the winner.

The USA Basketball 3×3 Women’s Selection Committee includes: Demings, Carol Callan(USA Basketball Women’s National Team director) and Kareem Maddox.

## Roster Named for USA Basketball Women’s 3x3 Olympic Qualifying Team

Mon, Feb 17, 2020, 9:34 PM

/

USA Basketball

![Image 18](https://cdn.wnba.com/sites/4/2020/02/Kelsye-Cover.jpg)  

The four-member rosters today were announced for the [USA Basketball Men’s and Women’s 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament Teams](https://www.usab.com/news-events/news/2020/02/3x3-oqt-teams.aspx) that will compete in the 2020 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament March 18-22 in Bengaluru, India, where the top three finishing men’s and women’s teams will earn berths into the 2020 Tokyo Olympic Games.

Named to the USA women’s team were current WNBA players: Napheesa Collier (Minnesota Lynx/O’Fallon, Mo.), Stefanie Dolson (Chicago Sky/Port Jervis, N.Y.), Allisha Gray (Dallas Wings/Sandersville, Ga.) and Kelsey Plum (Las Vegas Aces/Poway, Calif.).

The rosters were selected by the USA Basketball 3×3 Selection Committees following Feb. 12-15 training camps in Chicago that featured 11 female and 16 male hopefuls.

“USA Basketball is grateful to all of the athletes who attended training camp and competed for a roster spot,” said Jay Demings, USA Basketball Youth & Sport Development director and member of the USA Basketball 3×3 Men’s and Women’s Selection Committees. “It was a very talented field for both the men and women, and the committees had a very difficult task in selecting these teams. In the end, we are confident in the abilities of the eight players and the strength of the teams overall. Now, it is on to the very important task of qualifying the USA for the 3×3 Olympic basketball competition in Tokyo.”

The USA women earned their spot in the FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament by virtue of their status on the FIBA 3×3 world rankings as of this past November.

As per FIBA regulations, all teams taking part in the 2020 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament must include on their rosters at least two athletes who are ranked among the federation’s top 10 FIBA 3×3 athletes.

On the women’s side Collier, Dolson and Plum also are members of the 2020 USA Basketball Women’s National Team and have won gold medals with USA Basketball.

Additionally, Collier won gold at the 2014 Youth Olympic Games, which is a 3×3 competition.

The 2020 Olympics for the first time will feature the inclusion of 3×3 basketball with eight men’s and eight women’s teams competing for gold July 25-29 in Tokyo.

On the women’s side, Russia, China, Mongolia and Romania earned Olympic bids by virtue of their top FIBA 3×3 world rankings.

Twenty men’s and 20 women’s teams will compete for three Olympic qualifying berths in the March 18-22 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournaments.

The USA women at the FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament will play in Group A with France, Germany, Uruguay and Indonesia. Group B includes Iran, Japan, Ukraine, Turkmenistan and Australia. Group C features Netherlands, Estonia, Belarus, Hungary and Sri Lanka. And, in Group D will be Italy, Taipei, Switzerland, Spain and host India.

The eighth and final Olympic 3×3 spots will be awarded based on FIBA’s universality clause, which is designed to offer an Olympic 3×3 berth to one country in the men’s and the women’s tournament who did not have a team at the 2012 or 2016 Olympic basketball tournaments. The FIBA Universality Qualifying Tournaments, which will be held in April 2020 in Budapest Hungary, will include six men’s and six women’s teams. The top men’s and women’s finishers will advance to the Olympics.

An exciting and fast-paced game, 3×3 officially was unveiled in international competition at the 2010 Youth Olympic Games and since has become a fan favorite at FIBA 3×3 World Cup events. Played on a half court with a 10-minute clock, and a 12-second shot clock, the first team to 21 points, or the team in the lead at the end of regulation, is the winner.

The USA Basketball 3×3 Women’s Selection Committee includes: Demings, Carol Callan(USA Basketball Women’s National Team director) and Kareem Maddox.

# A Star-Studded Roster: Meet The 12 Members Of The U.S. Olympic Women’s Basketball Team

Share:

[Share on Facebook, opens in a new tab](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.teamusa.com%2Fnews%2F2021%2Fjune%2F21%2Fmeet-the-12-members-of-the-us-olympic-womens-basketball-team)[Share on X, opens in a new tab](https://x.com/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.teamusa.com%2Fnews%2F2021%2Fjune%2F21%2Fmeet-the-12-members-of-the-us-olympic-womens-basketball-team)[Share on Threads, opens in a new tab](https://www.threads.net/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.teamusa.com%2Fnews%2F2021%2Fjune%2F21%2Fmeet-the-12-members-of-the-us-olympic-womens-basketball-team&text=A%20Star-Studded%20Roster%3A%20Meet%20The%2012%20Members%20Of%20The%20U.S.%20Olympic%20Women%E2%80%99s%20Basketball%20Team)

Jun 21, 2021, 4:17 AM EDT
by Todd Kortemeier, Chrös McDougall

Just half of the 12-player roster for the U.S. Olympic women’s [basketball](https://www.usab.com/) team has previous Olympic experience, but that experience equals 15 gold medals.  
  
  
USA Basketball announced the experienced squad Monday morning on NBC’s TODAY show. Some of the most decorated stars of international basketball such as Sue Bird and Diana Taurasi are back for a fifth Olympic Games, joining with other Olympic veterans and six first-time Olympians to go after Team USA’s seventh consecutive gold medal. The U.S. squad also has a combined 19 FIBA World Cup gold medals, making one of the most experienced teams in the world.  
  
  
“USA Basketball has never been in a better place,” said U.S. head coach Dawn Staley in a news release. “… I’m so proud to be the coach of Team USA and like all of the coaches, support staff, and our players, I can’t wait to make America proud this summer.”  
  
  
Here’s a closer look at the 12 players looking to continue the U.S. gold medal standard in Tokyo.

#### Ariel Atkins

## Ariel Atkins

  
  
  

![Image 3: atkins ariel Updated](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1684894605/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/atkins_ariel_020820_1440x810_Updated.jpg)

[_Ariel Atkins_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/ariel-atkins-857611)_plays during the FIBA Women's Olympic Qualifying Tournament 2020 Group A match on February 8, 2020 in Belgrade, Serbia_

One of a trio of three 24-year-olds on the team — though she'll turn 25 in Tokyo — Atkins is making not only her Olympic debut but her senior international debut. The Washington Mystics’ guard does have USA [Basketball](https://www.usab.com/) experience on the youth side, winning gold with the 2014 FIBAAmericas Under-18 Championship team as well as participating in numerous training camps.

#### Sue Bird

## Sue Bird

  
  
  

![Image 4: Bird Sue](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1695393228/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/Bird_Sue_2019_1440x810.jpg)

[_Sue Bird_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/sue-bird)_poses during the Team USA Tokyo 2020 Olympic shoot on November 23, 2019 in West Hollywood, California._

For the fifth Olympic Games in a row, Team USA will be able to count on one of the living legends of the sport. The 40-year-old Seattle Storm point guard and her four gold medals are back for another run, and the U.S. has never lost an Olympic game with her on the team. The U.S. in fact is 142-6 all-time with Bird and has also won four FIBA World Cup gold medals and one bronze medal. Those nine total medals are the most for any [basketball](https://www.usab.com/) player in the world.

#### Tina Charles

## Tina Charles

  
  
  

![Image 5: charles tina Updated](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1695393230/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/charles_tina_072516_1440x810_Updated.jpg)

[_Tina Charles_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/tina-charles-828575)_plays in the second half of a game against the USA Select Team at Galen Center on July 25, 2016 in Los Angeles, California._

The center is back for a third Olympic Games, hoping to add to her resume of two Olympic gold medals and three World Cup gold medals. The former WNBA No. 1 overall draft pick, Charles was the 2012 league MVP and is a seven-time All-Star. Now 32, Charles made the senior national team for the first time in 2009 and was named USA [Basketball](https://www.usab.com/) Female Athlete of the Year that season.

#### Napheesa Collier

## Napheesa Collier

  
  
  

![Image 6: collier napheesa Updated](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1695393233/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/collier_napheesa_092720_1440x810_Updated.jpg)

[_Napheesa Collier_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/napheesa-collier-833890)_dribbles during Game Three of their Third Round playoff against the Seattle Storm at Feld Entertainment Center on September 27, 2020 in Palmetto, Florida._

Collier, 24, is making her Olympic debut but is a Youth Olympian from 2014, where she played 3x3. Collier has international experience in 3x3 and 5x5, compiling a total record of 49-1 across both. The 6-foot-1 guard-forward most recently won a gold medal in 5x5 with the national team at the 2019 FIBA AmeriCup. She was a WNBA All-Star and Rookie of the Year for the Minnesota Lynx in 2019.

#### Skylar Diggins-Smith

## Skylar Diggins-Smith

  
  
  

![Image 7: diggins smith skylar Updated](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1695393235/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/diggins_smith_skylar_020220_1440x810_Updated.jpg)

[_Skylar Diggins-Smith_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/skylar-diggins-smith-1194916)_handles the ball against the Louisville Cardinals during an exhibition game at KFC YUM! Center on February 2, 2020 in Louisville, Kentucky._

Diggins-Smith was part of the team that won the first-ever FIBA 3x3 World Cup in 2012, but will be making her 5x5 senior debut at a major tournament. Diggins-Smith, who will turn 31 in Tokyo, does have gold medals from youth teams including the 2009 FIBA U19 World Championship team. The guard is a four-time WNBA All-Star now playing with the Phoenix Mercury.

#### Sylvia Fowles

## Sylvia Fowles

  
  
  

![Image 8: fowles sylvia Updated](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1695393236/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/fowles_sylvia_012720_1440x810_Updated.jpg)

[_Sylvia Fowles_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/sylvia-fowles-908076)_looks on during USA Women's National Team Winter Tour 2020 game between the United States and the UConn Huskies at The XL Center on January 27, 2020 in Hartford, Connecticut._

Fowles will become just the sixth U.S. [basketball](https://www.usab.com/) player, male or female, to play in four Olympic Games. The 35-year-old Minnesota Lynx center is a WNBA MVP and two-time Finals MVP and is known as a defensive force. Fowles has won three Defensive Player of the Year awards and is a six-time All-Star. Fowles most recently won an international gold medal on the 2019 AmeriCup team, winning the tournament MVP award.

#### Chelsea Gray

## Chelsea Gray

  
  
  

![Image 9: gray chelsea Updated](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1695393238/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/gray_chelsea_012720_1440x810_Updated.jpg)

[_Chelsea Gray_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/chelsea-gray-1194920)_drives in for a shot during USA Women's National Team Winter Tour 2020 game between the United States and the UConn Huskies at The XL Center on January 27, 2020 in Hartford, Connecticut_

Gray, 28, is headed to her first major international championship. That’s fitting for the 5-foot-11 guard who has made a nice career for herself after being selected 11th overall from Duke in the 2014 WNBA Draft. Now a three-time WNBA All-Star and 2016 league champ with the Los Angeles Sparks, Gray has taken part in several national team training camps and exhibitions but never a major tournament in the red, white and blue.

#### Brittney Griner

## Brittney Griner

  
  
  

![Image 10: griner brittney Updated](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1695393241/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/griner_brittney_072516_1440x810_Updated.jpg)

[_Brittney Griner_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/brittney-griner-907854)_keeps control of the ball during the game at Galen Center on July 25, 2016 in Los Angeles, California._

Team USA’s towering inside presence, the 6-foot-9 Griner is going for her fourth major international championship at age 30. Also a 2016 Olympic gold medalist, Griner helped the U.S. to titles at the 2014 and 2018 World Cups, and was the player of the game in the latter. Also a national champion at Baylor, Griner is a member of the exclusive club of 11 women who have won an Olympic, World Cup, WNBA and NCAA title.

#### Jewell Loyd

## Jewell Loyd

  
  
  

![Image 11: loyd jewell Updated](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1695393243/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/loyd_jewell_020820_1440x810_Updated.jpg)

[_Jewell Loyd_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/jewell-loyd-997397)_celebrates during the FIBA Women's Olympic Qualifying Tournament 2020 Group A match at Aleksandar Nikolic Hall on February 8, 2020 in Belgrade, Serbia_

One of the relatively green members of this loaded U.S. team, at least in terms in international experience, Loyd nonetheless heads to Tokyo with a 2018 World Cup title under her belt, as well as two WNBA titles for the Seattle Storm. Loyd, a 27-year-old guard, also won the 2014 3x3 World Cup with Team USA, making her the first person to win that tournament at the 3x3 and 5x5 levels.

#### Breanna Stewart

## Breanna Stewart

  
  
  

![Image 12: Stewart Breanna](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1695393245/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/Stewart_Breanna_2019_1440x810.jpg)

[_Breanna Stewart_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/breanna-stewart-816374)_poses during the Team USA Tokyo 2020 Olympic shoot on November 23, 2019 in West Hollywood, California._

A national team player going back to her high school days, Stewart, now 26, is headed to her second Olympics with Team USA. The former UConn star who now plays for the WNBA’s Seattle Storm is among the group of just 11 women to have won an Olympic gold medal, FIBA World Cup gold medal, WNBA title and NCAA title. Standing 6-foot-4, the forward-center was named tournament MVP at the 2018 World Cup after averaging 16.3 points, 6.3 rebounds and 2.5 assists per game, all on 58 percent shooting.  

#### Diana Taurasi

## Diana Taurasi

  
  
  

![Image 13: taurasi diana Updated](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1695393247/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/taurasi_diana_081816_1440x810_Updated.jpg)

[_Diana Taurasi_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/diana-taurasi-915847)_dribbles the ball during the USA Vs France Women's_[_Basketball_](https://www.usab.com/)_Semifinal at Carioca Arena1 on August 18, 2016 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil._

Treading dangerously into GOAT territory, Taurasi, a 6-foot guard, is headed to her fifth Olympics, and that’s barely scratching the surface. At 39 years old, Taurasi is also a three-time World Cup champ, three-time WNBA MVP and six-time EuroLeague winner. Then there are the individual honors: 1 WNBA MVP, 2 WNBA Finals MVPs, 3 EuroLeague Finals MVPs, 4 USA Basketball Female Athlete of the Year honors. Oh yeah, she’s also the WNBA’s all-time leading scorer. Need we go on?

#### A'ja Wilson

## A'ja Wilson

  
  
  

![Image 14: Wilson Aja](https://res.cloudinary.com/usopc-prod/image/upload/v1695393249/TeamUSA%20Assets/Migration/Wilson_Aja_2019_1440x810.jpg)

[_A'ja Wilson_](https://www.teamusa.com/profiles/a-ja-wilson-837897)_poses during the Team USA Tokyo 2020 Olympic shoot on November 23, 2019 in West Hollywood, California._

One of the WNBA’s brightest young stars, Wilson, 24, will make her Olympic debut after previously helping lead Team USA to gold at the 2018 World Cup. She was the youngest member of that team and averaged 10 points and 4 assists throughout the tournament. The 2020 WNBA MVP with the Las Vegas Aces, Wilson, a 6-5 forward, brings a perfect 47-0 national team record to Tokyo.
